Cattle breeds.Angus: Angus cattle are naturally hornless, black or red, and the breed's marbled meat made it a favorite of steakhouses worldwide.
Cattle breeds.Hereford: Herefords are red-bodied cattle with white faces, bred in England, and they thrive on grass in tough, open range country.
Cattle breeds.Holstein: Holsteins are the black-and-white dairy champions of the world, and a top cow can give over 30 liters of milk a day.
Cattle breeds.Jersey: Jersey cattle come from the island of Jersey, and their milk is rich in butterfat, ideal for cream and cheese.
Cattle breeds.Guernsey: Guernsey cows produce golden-tinted milk, colored by a high level of beta-carotene, and they hail from a Channel island.
Cattle breeds.Texas Longhorn: Texas Longhorns carry horns that can span well over a meter and a half, and descended from cattle brought by Spanish settlers.
Cattle breeds.Highland: Highland cattle are shaggy, long-horned Scots with a double coat that lets them live happily outdoors in wintry Scotland.
Cattle breeds.Brahman: Brahman cattle descend from Indian zebu and handle heat and insects far better than most European breeds, thanks to their humped shoulders.
Cattle breeds.Charolais: Charolais are creamy-white French beef cattle, big and muscular, from the Charolles region of Burgundy.
Cattle breeds.Wagyu: Wagyu cattle are Japanese breeds known for intensely marbled beef, one of the world's priciest steaks.
Cattle breeds.Limousin: Limousin cattle from central France are golden-red and prized for lean, tender beef.
Cattle breeds.Merino: Merinos are sheep known for fine wool, so they're not cattle.
Cattle breeds.Suffolk: Suffolk is a black-faced sheep breed from England, raised mostly for meat, not cattle.
Cattle breeds.Berkshire: Berkshire is a prized pig breed from England, famous for flavorful, dark pork, and it is not cattle.
Cattle breeds.Leghorn: Leghorns are white chickens from Italy, and they are among the best layers, producing roughly 280 eggs a year.
Cattle breeds.Rhode Island Red: Rhode Island Reds are hardy brown chickens and the state bird of Rhode Island, not a cattle breed.
Cattle breeds.Yorkshire: Yorkshire pigs, also called Large Whites, are among the most common pig breeds in the world.
Cattle breeds.Clydesdale: Clydesdales are heavy draft horses from Scotland, and horses don't belong in the cattle yard.
Cattle breeds.Nubian: Nubians are floppy-eared dairy goats, known for rich milk and a Roman nose, not cattle.
Cattle breeds.Angora: Angora can mean a long-haired goat, rabbit or cat, and the soft fiber from angora goats is called mohair.
Cattle breeds.Tamworth: Tamworths are reddish pigs from England and one of the oldest pig breeds, not cattle.
Cattle breeds.Bantam: Bantams are miniature chickens, often a third to a half the size of standard breeds.
Cattle breeds.Silkie: Silkies are fluffy chickens with fur-like feathers, black skin and, oddly, five toes instead of four.
Cattle breeds.Dorper: Dorper sheep were developed in South Africa by crossing a Dorset with a Blackhead Persian, and they shed rather than needing shearing.

Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Acorn: Squirrels often forget some buried acorns, and the forgotten ones sprout, so squirrels quietly plant oak forests.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Walnut: A squirrel can smell a buried walnut under snow, and they sometimes pretend to bury nuts to fool onlookers.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Hazelnut: Hazelnuts are favorites for squirrels, and each nut is typically stashed in its own small hole.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Pecan: Squirrels bury pecans in lots of separate spots, a strategy called scatter hoarding that spreads the risk of theft.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Hickory nut: Hickory nuts have such hard shells that only strong squirrel teeth can open them, and their teeth never stop growing.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Chestnut: Sweet chestnuts are starchy and low in fat, so they spoil faster than acorns, and squirrels often eat them right away.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Beechnut: Beech trees fruit heavily only every few years, a mast year that feeds squirrels and fuels population booms.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Peanut: Though technically a legume that grows underground, peanuts are readily buried by squirrels in parks.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Pine cone: Squirrels hoard whole pine cones in stashes called middens, which can grow to hold hundreds of cones.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Bone: Dogs bury bones, not squirrels, whose diet is mostly seeds, nuts, and fungi.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Carrot: A squirrel doesn't typically bury carrots, since root vegetables spoil quickly, though squirrels do eat plant roots.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Cheese: Cheese would spoil in the ground, and squirrels live on nuts, seeds, and fungi, not dairy.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Banana: Fruits like bananas spoil too fast to store, so squirrels would never bury them.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Hay: Hay is bedding and food for grazers like horses and rabbits, not a squirrel hoard.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Fish: Squirrels are mostly vegetarian, so fish is not on their menu, though they will sometimes nibble a bone for calcium.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Worm: Squirrels don't hoard worms; rotting food would attract pests, and squirrels prefer storable seeds.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Bamboo: Bamboo is the diet of giant pandas, which live in China, not a squirrel hoard.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Eucalyptus: Koalas feed on these leaves, which are poisonous to most animals, and squirrels don't store them.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Honey: Bears and honey badgers raid beehives, but squirrels don't hoard honey.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Plankton: Plankton are tiny drifting sea organisms, the food of whales, and no squirrel's.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Krill: Krill are shrimp-like crustaceans, eaten by whales, and a squirrel would never get near them.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Steak: Squirrels do not stockpile meat, since they are largely herbivores with a diet of nuts and seeds.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Lettuce: Leafy greens wilt and rot quickly, so they make bad winter storage for any hoarder.
Things a squirrel might bury for winter.Seaweed: Seaweed grows in the sea and feeds animals like sea urchins, not squirrels.

Greek islands.Crete: Greece's largest island and the home of the Minoans, Europe's earliest advanced civilisation, and the legendary Minotaur's labyrinth at Knossos.
Greek islands.Rhodes: Once guarded by the Colossus, one of the Seven Wonders, a giant bronze statue that stood around 280 BC until an earthquake toppled it.
Greek islands.Corfu: An island in the Ionian Sea, whose old town is on UNESCO's list. It has Venetian, French and British architecture; the Durrells made it famous in books.
Greek islands.Santorini: A caldera island formed by one of history's largest volcanic eruptions around 1600 BC, whose blast may have helped end Minoan civilisation.
Greek islands.Mykonos: A Cyclades island, famous for windmills, whitewashed streets, and pelicans that wander the harbour. It's a famous party hotspot.
Greek islands.Lesbos: The island's name gave us 'lesbian', because the poet Sappho was born here in the 7th century BC.
Greek islands.Kos: Hippocrates, the father of medicine, was born here, and the plane tree under which he supposedly taught still stands in the town.
Greek islands.Zakynthos: An Ionian island and home to loggerhead sea turtles that nest on its beaches. It is also known as Zante.
Greek islands.Naxos: The largest of the Cyclades, an island of lush valleys. In myth, Dionysus was said to have wed Ariadne here.
Greek islands.Ithaca: Odysseus's home island in Homer's epic, which took him ten years to reach on the way home from Troy. It's in the Ionian Sea.
Greek islands.Cyprus: A trap: Cyprus is a Greek-speaking island but a separate country, and it lies far to the east, closer to Syria than to Greece.
Greek islands.Malta: A trap: an independent island country, so it is not Greek, and lies south of Sicily. The Knights of St John ruled it for centuries.
Greek islands.Sicily: The Mediterranean's biggest island, but Italian. Greeks colonized it in ancient times, but it's not a Greek island.
Greek islands.Sardinia: A trap: the Mediterranean's second-largest island is Italian, with ancient nuraghe stone towers, so it is not a Greek island.
Greek islands.Corsica: A trap: this island belongs to France and is Napoleon's birthplace, so it is not one of the Greek islands.
Greek islands.Ibiza: A trap: a Spanish island in the Balearics, famed for its nightclubs and old town. It is not Greek.
Greek islands.Majorca: A trap: the largest of Spain's Balearic Islands, famed for its beaches and the Tramuntana mountains. It is not Greek.
Greek islands.Capri: A trap: an Italian island in the Bay of Naples, famous for its Blue Grotto and Roman emperor Tiberius's villa. Not Greek.
Greek islands.Elba: A tiny Italian island in Tuscany, where Napoleon was first exiled in 1814. It's not Greek.
Greek islands.Gozo: A trap: Malta's smaller sister island, said by some to be Homer's Ogygia, where Calypso held Odysseus. It's not Greek.
Greek islands.Hvar: A trap: a sunny Croatian island in the Adriatic, famous for lavender fields and Venetian-era towns. It is not Greek.
Greek islands.Djerba: A Tunisian island off Africa's coast. It's a legendary land of the lotus-eaters from the Odyssey, but not Greek.
Greek islands.Menorca: A trap: a quieter Spanish Balearic island, a UNESCO biosphere reserve. It is not Greek.
Greek islands.Bornholm: A trap: a Danish island in the Baltic Sea, far to the north of Greece, known for its round churches. It is not Greek.

Countries that drive on the left.UK: British law has favored the left since an 1835 highway act, though the habit is far older.
Countries that drive on the left.Ireland: Traffic keeps to the left as in Britain, a habit inherited when the whole island was under British rule.
Countries that drive on the left.Japan: It drives on the left, and Japan's used right-hand-drive cars are exported to many other left-driving countries.
Countries that drive on the left.India: The left is the rule here, a legacy of the British Raj, in a country with the world's biggest road network after the USA.
Countries that drive on the left.Australia: Australia drives on the left like Britain, and its cars are right-hand drive. Roads in the outback can run for hundreds of kilometers without a bend.
Countries that drive on the left.New Zealand: It drives on the left, and many of its cars are secondhand imports from Japan.
Countries that drive on the left.South Africa: A left-hand driving country, a legacy of British rule, where most cars have the steering wheel on the right.
Countries that drive on the left.Thailand: Thailand drives on the left despite never having been colonized, and it adopted the rule early in the 20th century.
Countries that drive on the left.Indonesia: Left-hand traffic is the rule, even though its colonial rulers, the Dutch, drove on the right.
Countries that drive on the left.Malaysia: British colonial rule left Malaysia with left-hand traffic and right-hand-drive cars.
Countries that drive on the left.Kenya: Left-hand traffic here is a British colonial legacy, shared with its East African neighbors.
Countries that drive on the left.Jamaica: Jamaica drives on the left, a British inheritance, and the country is home to the world's fastest sprinter, Usain Bolt.
Countries that drive on the left.Cyprus: This Mediterranean island drives on the left, a legacy of British rule that ended in 1960.
Countries that drive on the left.Malta: Malta keeps left, a British legacy, and it is one of the few left-driving countries in the EU.
Countries that drive on the left.Singapore: Singapore drives on the left, and its heavy car taxes make owning a car very expensive.
Countries that drive on the left.USA: Wagon teamsters sitting on the left horse are credited with leading Americans to keep right.
Countries that drive on the left.Canada: Canada keeps right, but British Columbia switched from the left only in 1920 and Newfoundland in 1947.
Countries that drive on the left.France: The French keep right, a habit often credited to Napoleon's armies spreading it around Europe.
Countries that drive on the left.China: Mainland China drives on the right, though former colonies Hong Kong and Macau keep to the left.
Countries that drive on the left.Brazil: Brazil drives on the right, like most of Latin America.
Countries that drive on the left.Egypt: Egyptians drive on the right, like most of the Middle East and Africa's north.
Countries that drive on the left.Russia: Russia drives on the right, yet in the Far East, many cars are right-hand-drive imports from Japan.
Countries that drive on the left.South Korea: South Korea switched to the right in 1946, ending the left-hand traffic imposed during Japanese rule.
Countries that drive on the left.Sweden: Sweden switched from left to right overnight on 3 September 1967, known as Dagen H.

Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Australia: Wholly in the south, it has summer at Christmas. The country is also the only continent that is a single nation, and its seasons are flipped from Europe's.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.New Zealand: Lies entirely south of the equator, and Auckland is about 37 degrees south. Its sheep outnumber people, roughly five to one in recent decades.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Argentina: Argentina stretches south to Tierra del Fuego, one of the world's southernmost inhabited areas. Ushuaia calls itself the end of the world.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Chile: A long ribbon, over 4,000 km north to south, all in the Southern Hemisphere. It holds the Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.South Africa: The country's seasons are reversed from Europe's, so winter runs June to August. Cape Town is far south, near Africa's southwestern tip.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Madagascar: The big island lies between about 12 and 25 degrees south. It split from India about 88 million years ago, so most of its species are found nowhere else.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Uruguay: Uruguay lies at 30 to 35 degrees south, entirely in the Southern Hemisphere. It's one of South America's smallest countries, and it's known for gauchos and beef.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Paraguay: Paraguay is landlocked and south of the equator. It's a rare country where the Guaraní language, alongside Spanish, is spoken by most of the population.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Bolivia: All of Bolivia is south of the equator. It's landlocked, with two capitals, La Paz and Sucre, and it holds the world's biggest salt flat, the Salar de Uyuni.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Namibia: Namibia lies between about 17 and 29 degrees south. It's one of the least densely populated countries, with an old desert, the Namib, running along its coast.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Botswana: The country sits at 18 to 27 degrees south, entirely in the Southern Hemisphere. Most of its land is the Kalahari, and its Okavango Delta floods in the dry season.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Zimbabwe: Zimbabwe sits at 15 to 22 degrees south. Victoria Falls, on its border with Zambia, is locally called Mosi-oa-Tunya, the smoke that thunders.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Angola: Angola is south of the equator, including its Cabinda enclave. It sits roughly between 5 and 18 degrees south.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Brazil: The equator crosses northern Brazil, so the country straddles both hemispheres. Most of it, including Rio and São Paulo, is in the south.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Ecuador: The country is named for the equator, which runs through it, so part of it lies north. Quito is just slightly south of the line.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Indonesia: The equator runs straight through Indonesia, splitting its islands, so it lies in both hemispheres.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Kenya: The equator runs through central Kenya, so a good part of the country is north of the line, including Mount Kenya's foothills.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Colombia: Most of Colombia, including Bogotá, is north of the equator, though its southern tip dips just below, near the Amazon.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.India: India lies north of the equator, between roughly 8 and 37 degrees north, so it's entirely in the Northern Hemisphere.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Egypt: Egypt lies in the Northern Hemisphere, between about 22 and 31 degrees north, with the Nile flowing north to the sea.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Mexico: Mexico lies fully in the Northern Hemisphere, between about 14 and 32 degrees north.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Nigeria: Nigeria lies in the Northern Hemisphere, between about 4 and 14 degrees north, so not entirely southern at all.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Thailand: Thailand lies north of the equator, between about 6 and 21 degrees north, and not in the Southern Hemisphere.
Entirely in the Southern Hemisphere.Philippines: The Philippines are north of the equator. Its southernmost islands are at about 5 degrees north.

Places in the Republic of Ireland.Dublin: Vikings settled beside a tidal pool called "dubh linn", Irish for black pool, and that dark water gave Ireland's capital its name.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Cork: Ireland's second city grew on islands in the River Lee, and locals jokingly insist it is the real capital of the country.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Galway: This Atlantic city gave its name to the Claddagh ring, whose clasped hands, heart and crown stand for friendship, love and loyalty.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Limerick: A Shannon-side city, and also the name of the five-line comic verse. Whether the poem really comes from the city is still debated.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Cliffs of Moher: Sheer Atlantic cliffs in County Clare that rise to about 214 metres and draw roughly a million visitors a year.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Ring of Kerry: A scenic loop of about 180 km around the Iveragh Peninsula. Tour coaches traditionally drive it counter-clockwise to avoid jams on narrow bends.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Killarney: Its national park, created in 1932 from a donated estate, was Ireland's first and holds lakes, mountains and native red deer.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Blarney Castle: Kissing the Blarney Stone is said to grant the gift of eloquent flattery, but you must lean backward over a drop to reach it.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Kilkenny: A medieval city on the River Nore nicknamed the Marble City, for the polished black limestone quarried nearby.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Waterford: Founded by Vikings in 914, it is often called Ireland's oldest city, and it gave its name to the famous cut crystal.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Connemara: A wild western region of bogs, lakes and mountains where Irish is still spoken daily and a hardy native pony breed roams.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Dingle: This peninsula harbour town became famous for Fungie, a bottlenose dolphin who lived in the bay and greeted boats for decades from 1984.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Aran Islands: Three rocky islands off Galway where Irish is the everyday language. The cream cable-knit sweaters are their best-known export.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Belfast: The capital of Northern Ireland, so part of the United Kingdom, not the Republic. The Titanic was built in its shipyards.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Giant's Causeway: About 40,000 basalt columns on the Antrim coast. It is in Northern Ireland, so it falls outside the Republic.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Armagh: Both the Catholic and Anglican churches of all Ireland are headquartered here, yet the city lies in Northern Ireland.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Isle of Man: It sits in the Irish Sea but is a self-governing Crown dependency, belonging neither to the Republic nor to the UK.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Glasgow: A big Scottish city with strong Irish roots from migration, but it lies across the sea in Scotland, not in Ireland.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Liverpool: Millions of Irish people passed through this English port, and its accent shows Irish influence, but it is in England.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Holyhead: The Welsh port where ferries leave for Dublin. It ends the Irish route, but the town itself is in Wales.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Cardiff: The Welsh capital lies across the Irish Sea, with no Irish connection beyond ferries and rugby rivalry.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Anglesey: A Welsh island whose port of Holyhead links to Dublin by ferry, which makes it a trap: close to Ireland, yet Welsh.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Newry: This city straddles the old border between Down and Armagh, and sits in Northern Ireland, not the Republic.
Places in the Republic of Ireland.Enniskillen: A Fermanagh town built on an island between the two parts of Lough Erne, and part of Northern Ireland.

Major languages of India.Hindi: India's most widely spoken language, written in the Devanagari script, and an official language of the Union government alongside English.
Major languages of India.Bengali: Rabindranath Tagore wrote in it and won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature, the first for a non-European.
Major languages of India.Tamil: One of the world's oldest living classical languages, with literature stretching back more than 2,000 years.
Major languages of India.Telugu: Spoken in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, it is nicknamed the Italian of the East for its vowel-ending words.
Major languages of India.Marathi: The language of Maharashtra, whose capital Mumbai is India's financial centre and film capital.
Major languages of India.Gujarati: Mahatma Gandhi's mother tongue, spoken by millions in Gujarat and across the Indian diaspora.
Major languages of India.Punjabi: Written in Gurmukhi script in India, and unusual among Indo-European languages for being tonal.
Major languages of India.Kannada: The language of Karnataka and the tech hub Bengaluru, with a script that looks much like Telugu's.
Major languages of India.Malayalam: Spoken in Kerala, and its name is a palindrome, reading the same backward and forward.
Major languages of India.Odia: Recognised as a classical language in 2014, it is the language of Odisha on India's east coast.
Major languages of India.Urdu: It sounds almost identical to Hindi in everyday speech, but is written in a Persian-Arabic script.
Major languages of India.Thai: The language of Thailand, with five tones and its own script, not an Indian language.
Major languages of India.Tagalog: The basis of Filipino, the national language of the Philippines, not of India.
Major languages of India.Sinhala: The main language of Sri Lanka, with a looping script, and not one of India's major languages.
Major languages of India.Swahili: A Bantu language of East Africa with many Arabic loanwords, and unrelated to India's languages.
Major languages of India.Burmese: Spoken in Myanmar, with a round script, and a Sino-Tibetan language, not an Indian one.
Major languages of India.Malay: It is spoken in Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, not in India.
Major languages of India.Dzongkha: The national language of Bhutan, a Tibetan-related language that is not one of India's major tongues.
Major languages of India.Khmer: Cambodia's language has one of the longest alphabets in the world, with 74 characters. It isn't Indian.
Major languages of India.Javanese: The main language of Java in Indonesia, with a script derived from Indian origins, but spoken in Indonesia.
Major languages of India.Amharic: Ethiopia's working language, with the Ge'ez script, and not spoken in India.
Major languages of India.Vietnamese: Vietnam's tonal language, written in a Latin-based alphabet, and not an Indian language.
Major languages of India.Lao: Laos's national language, closely related to Thai, and not spoken in India.
Major languages of India.Korean: Written in Hangul, invented in the 15th century, and a language of the Korean peninsula.

Invertebrates.Octopus: A mollusc with no backbone, three hearts and blue blood. It can squeeze through any gap larger than its beak.
Invertebrates.Jellyfish: A soft-bodied cnidarian with no brain. One species, Turritopsis dohrnii, can revert to a juvenile stage and is nicknamed immortal.
Invertebrates.Starfish: An echinoderm lacking a brain and blood. It moves with hundreds of tiny tube feet, and has an eye at the tip of each arm.
Invertebrates.Spider: An arachnid, not an insect, with eight legs. Its silk is stronger than steel by weight.
Invertebrates.Earthworm: An annelid with five pairs of hearts, no lungs, and it breathes through its skin. Darwin studied worms for decades.
Invertebrates.Snail: A mollusc that can seal itself in its shell for years. It has a rasp-like tongue with thousands of tiny teeth.
Invertebrates.Crab: An arthropod with a hard shell and a sideways walk. It has ten legs, including the pincers.
Invertebrates.Lobster: An arthropod that keeps growing all its life. It molts its shell repeatedly, and it tastes with its feet.
Invertebrates.Squid: A mollusc with ten limbs and a brain wrapped around its throat. Its giant nerve fibers helped scientists first understand how nerves fire.
Invertebrates.Sea urchin: A spiny echinoderm that feeds with a five-part jaw called Aristotle's lantern, named after the philosopher who described it.
Invertebrates.Coral: Tiny colonial animals called polyps build reefs. Despite looking like rock or plants, coral is an animal.
Invertebrates.Sponge: The simplest animal, without organs, nerves or muscles. It filters water through pores and a body that can regrow from fragments.
Invertebrates.Butterfly: An insect that begins as a caterpillar. Inside the chrysalis, the caterpillar's body nearly dissolves before it reforms.
Invertebrates.Leech: An annelid with a sucker at each end and three jaws, whose saliva contains an anticoagulant. Doctors still use leeches after some surgeries.
Invertebrates.Seahorse: A trap: it's a fish with a backbone, so a vertebrate. The male carries the young.
Invertebrates.Eel: A trap: it looks like a snake but is a fish with a backbone and gills. European eels cross the Atlantic to breed.
Invertebrates.Snake: A trap: a reptile with a backbone running its whole length, with hundreds of vertebrae in some species, so it's a vertebrate.
Invertebrates.Frog: A trap: an amphibian with a backbone. It's a vertebrate, though its tadpole breathes through gills.
Invertebrates.Shark: A trap: its skeleton is cartilage, but sharks are still vertebrates, with a spine.
Invertebrates.Bat: A trap: the only mammal capable of true flight, and like all mammals it has a backbone, so it is a vertebrate.
Invertebrates.Turtle: A trap: a reptile whose backbone and ribs are fused to its shell, so it's a vertebrate, not a shelled invertebrate like a snail.
Invertebrates.Salamander: A trap: an amphibian with a backbone, and a vertebrate, though some species can regrow lost limbs and even parts of the heart.
Invertebrates.Penguin: A trap: a flightless bird that swims, but a bird has a backbone, so it is a vertebrate, unlike a squid or crab.
Invertebrates.Stingray: A trap: a flat cousin of sharks with a skeleton of cartilage and a spine, so it is a vertebrate, not an invertebrate.

Invented before the year 1900.Telephone: Alexander Graham Bell's 1876 patent set off a famous dispute over who invented it first, and his first call was to his assistant in the next room.
Invented before the year 1900.Printing press: Gutenberg's movable-type press of the 1450s made books cheap enough to spread literacy and ideas across Europe.
Invented before the year 1900.Steam engine: Early versions pumped water out of mines in the late 1600s, and James Watt's improvements powered the Industrial Revolution.
Invented before the year 1900.Telescope: First reported in the Netherlands in 1608, and Galileo's improved version a year later changed how we see the sky.
Invented before the year 1900.Microscope: Dutch lens makers of the late 1500s are credited with it, and Leeuwenhoek used his to discover microbes.
Invented before the year 1900.Stethoscope: A French doctor in 1816 rolled paper into a tube to avoid pressing his ear to a patient's chest, since it was a delicate situation.
Invented before the year 1900.Dynamite: Alfred Nobel patented it in 1867 by stabilizing nitroglycerin with clay, and the fortune funded the Nobel Prizes.
Invented before the year 1900.Electric battery: Alessandro Volta's 1800 stack of metal discs gave us the first steady electric current, and the volt is named for him.
Invented before the year 1900.Telegraph: The electric version from the 1830s and 1840s, with Morse code, sent messages across continents in minutes.
Invented before the year 1900.Barometer: Evangelista Torricelli made the first in the 1640s, and it's why we measure air pressure in millimeters of mercury.
Invented before the year 1900.Phonograph: Edison's 1877 machine recorded sound on tinfoil, and his first recording was reportedly Mary Had a Little Lamb.
Invented before the year 1900.Airplane: First flown by the Wright brothers in 1903, so it falls just after 1900.
Invented before the year 1900.Television: Philo Farnsworth demonstrated an electronic version in 1927, and a few decades later it was in living rooms.
Invented before the year 1900.Penicillin: Alexander Fleming noticed it in 1928, and it only became a mass-produced drug in the 1940s.
Invented before the year 1900.Microwave oven: A radar engineer reportedly noticed a chocolate bar melting in his pocket in the 1940s, leading to this kitchen device.
Invented before the year 1900.Laser: Theodore Maiman built the first working one in 1960 and it was once called a solution looking for a problem.
Invented before the year 1900.Transistor: Bell Labs created it in 1947, and billions of them now sit on a single computer chip.
Invented before the year 1900.Velcro: A Swiss engineer got the idea after picking burrs off his dog in the 1940s, and it's named for velvet and hook in French.
Invented before the year 1900.Jet engine: Frank Whittle and Hans von Ohain built the first ones in the 1930s, so it came after 1900.
Invented before the year 1900.Nylon: DuPont's Wallace Carothers invented it in the 1930s, and it made its fame as a stocking material.
Invented before the year 1900.Post-it note: Spencer Silver's weak glue from the 1960s was a failure until a colleague used it for hymnbook bookmarks.
Invented before the year 1900.Bubble wrap: It started in 1957 as an attempt to make textured wallpaper, not packaging.
Invented before the year 1900.MRI scanner: Developed in the 1970s, it uses strong magnets and radio waves to image the body without X-rays.
Invented before the year 1900.Teflon: Roy Plunkett discovered it by accident in 1938 while working with refrigerant gases.

Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Apollo 11: The 1969 mission put the first humans on the Moon, and its computer had less power than a modern pocket calculator.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Voyager 1: Launched in 1977, it is the most distant human-made object, now in interstellar space, carrying a golden record of Earth's sounds.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Sputnik: The Soviet 1957 satellite was the first in orbit, and its simple beeping signal startled the world and began the Space Race.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Vostok 1: In 1961 it carried Yuri Gagarin on the first human spaceflight, a trip that lasted only 108 minutes.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Cassini: It orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017 and ended by diving into the planet, to avoid contaminating moons that might harbor life.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Skylab: America's first space station, launched in 1973, was damaged on takeoff and saved by a makeshift sunshade.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Mir: The Soviet and then Russian space station orbited for 15 years until 2001, and it hosted long stays like Valeri Polyakov's 437 days.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Columbia: The first space shuttle to reach orbit, in 1981, and it was lost in 2003 on its return.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Challenger: The shuttle was lost 73 seconds after liftoff in 1986, and Christa McAuliffe was meant to be the first teacher in space.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).New Horizons: It flew past Pluto in 2015 after a nine-year trip and sent back close-up images of its heart-shaped plain.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Pioneer 10: In 1973 it was the first spacecraft to fly past Jupiter, and it carried a plaque showing humankind.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Crew Dragon: Han Solo's ship brags it made the Kessel Run in under twelve parsecs, a famous slip, since a parsec measures distance, not time.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Soyuz: The Firefly-class ship from the TV series Firefly and the film named after it, crewed by smugglers on the fringe of space.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Millennium Falcon: Han Solo's smuggling ship from Star Wars, famous for making the Kessel Run in under twelve parsecs.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Serenity: The ship from the TV show Firefly, which is named for a kind of small Firefly-class transport.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Galactica: The warship from Battlestar Galactica, the last of its kind that leads a fleet of survivors.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Death Star: The Empire's moon-sized space station in Star Wars, with a fatal flaw in an exhaust port.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Nostromo: The Alien cargo tug whose crew meets the xenomorph, named for the Joseph Conrad novel.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).TARDIS: A time machine from Doctor Who that is bigger inside, disguised as a police box.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Heart of Gold: Starship from Douglas Adams' Hitchhiker's Guide, powered by the Infinite Improbability Drive.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Rocinante: The ship of The Expanse, a corvette-class ship named after Don Quixote's horse.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).Red Dwarf: The mining ship in the British sitcom Red Dwarf, whose crew is the last human alive.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).X-wing: Luke Skywalker's snub-nosed fighter in Star Wars, which destroyed the Death Star.
Real spacecraft (not science fiction).TIE fighter: The Empire's twin-ion-engine fighters from Star Wars, known for their eerie scream.

Things in our solar system.The Sun: Our star holds about 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass, and it is so large that over a million Earths could fit inside.
Things in our solar system.Ceres: The first asteroid ever found, in 1801, it holds about a third of the belt's mass and was later promoted to dwarf planet.
Things in our solar system.Pluto: It was a planet until 2006, when it was reclassified as a dwarf planet, and its giant moon Charon makes it almost a double system.
Things in our solar system.Halley's Comet: Its 76-year orbit made it the first comet proved to return, and it is the best-known one visible to the naked eye. Next due in 2061.
Things in our solar system.Kuiper Belt: A doughnut of icy bodies beyond Neptune, home to Pluto and many other dwarf planets, and it's the source of many short-period comets.
Things in our solar system.Asteroid belt: Millions of rocky bodies between Mars and Jupiter, yet they'd add up to less than the Moon's mass, so spacecraft pass through safely.
Things in our solar system.Oort Cloud: A vast, theoretical shell of icy bodies that may reach a light-year or more out, believed to be the source of long-period comets.
Things in our solar system.Titan: Saturn's biggest moon has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane, and the Huygens probe landed there in 2005.
Things in our solar system.Europa: Jupiter's moon has an ocean under its icy crust that may hold more water than all of Earth's, making it a top target in the search for life.
Things in our solar system.Phobos: This tiny Martian moon orbits so close that it circles Mars in about 7 hours, faster than the planet spins.
Things in our solar system.Vesta: The second-most massive object in the asteroid belt, it was visited by Dawn and is bright enough to be seen with the naked eye.
Things in our solar system.Charon: Pluto's largest moon is about half its planet's size, so the two circle a point in space between them.
Things in our solar system.Ganymede: The largest moon in the solar system is bigger than Mercury and is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field.
Things in our solar system.Sirius: The brightest star in our night sky is about 8.6 light-years away, so it isn't part of our solar system.
Things in our solar system.Polaris: The North Star is a distant supergiant, not in the solar system, and it sits almost directly above Earth's north pole.
Things in our solar system.Betelgeuse: This red supergiant in Orion is so large that, put in the Sun's place, it would swallow the orbit of Mars.
Things in our solar system.Proxima Centauri: The nearest known star to the Sun, about 4.2 light-years away, is in a different system, not ours.
Things in our solar system.Andromeda: The nearest large galaxy, about 2.5 million light-years away, will one day collide with the Milky Way.
Things in our solar system.Orion Nebula: A glowing cloud of gas in Orion's sword, where new stars are forming, visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy star.
Things in our solar system.Alpha Centauri: A close double star at 4.4 light-years, and with Proxima it forms our nearest stellar neighbors, not our own system.
Things in our solar system.Pleiades: A star cluster known as the Seven Sisters, visible to the naked eye, and well outside the solar system.
Things in our solar system.Crab Nebula: The remains of a supernova seen by Chinese astronomers in 1054, and it sits in Taurus, far beyond our system.
Things in our solar system.Vega: A bright blue-white star about 25 light-years away, and it was once the north pole star and will be again.
Things in our solar system.TRAPPIST-1: A cool star about 40 light-years away with seven Earth-size planets, and it's an entirely different system.

Things a geologist carries in the field.Rock hammer: Geologists use a pointed-tip hammer for splitting rocks and getting fresh surfaces. Many carry one with a flat end for chipping and a pick end for prying.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Hand lens: A small magnifier, usually 10x, hung around the neck. It reveals the mineral grains that identify a rock.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Compass: A geologist's compass, often called a Brunton, also measures the tilt of rock layers. It's used for recording strike and dip.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Field notebook: Often waterproof. Geologists record observations on the spot, because the exact position and orientation of a rock matter as much as the rock.
Things a geologist carries in the field.GPS: Handheld GPS lets geologists mark sample sites precisely. Before satellites, they relied on maps and landmarks.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Acid bottle: A small bottle of dilute hydrochloric acid fizzes on limestone, since the acid reacts with calcite. It's the quick way to tell it from other rocks.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Streak plate: A rough ceramic tile. Rubbing a mineral across it leaves a powder streak whose color can differ from the mineral itself, as with hematite's red-brown.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Topographic map: A map with contour lines shows the shape of the land. Geologists mark the rock units they find directly onto it.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Chisel: Geologists use a chisel to get a sample out of hard rock or to cut thin samples from a layer. It's used with the hammer.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Sample bags: Rock samples are bagged and labeled with their location. Without the label, a rock is nearly worthless as evidence.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Stethoscope: Doctors use it to listen to hearts and lungs. Geologists have no need to listen to anything inside a body.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Telescope: A tool for astronomers, not for the field geologist. Geologists rely on a hand lens, which magnifies small things nearby, not far away.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Butterfly net: This belongs to an entomologist, who studies insects. A geologist is collecting rocks, not butterflies.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Bunsen burner: A laboratory tool needing a gas supply, so it doesn't go on field trips. Back in the lab, it's useful for testing how minerals melt.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Scalpel: A surgeon's or biologist's cutting tool. Geologists need something sturdier than a scalpel to split rock.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Fishing rod: A fishing rod suits an angler, not a rock hunter. Geologists might still carry one on a long field trip, but not for work.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Spacesuit: Astronauts wear spacesuits, and Apollo's geologist-astronaut Harrison Schmitt was a rare exception. On Earth, geologists wear boots and a hat.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Lab coat: A lab coat is meant for indoor laboratories. In the field, geologists prefer sturdy outdoor clothing and good boots.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Petri dish: A Petri dish is used in biology for growing cultures. It has no use in a rocky outcrop.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Syringe: A medical or lab tool for liquids. A geologist's field kit has no need for it.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Gavel: A gavel belongs to a judge or an auctioneer. It looks like a hammer, but it's for calling order, not splitting rock.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Weather balloon: Meteorologists release these to measure the upper atmosphere. Geologists focus on the ground beneath their feet.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Easel: An easel is for painters. Geologists do sketch outcrops, but they use a notebook, not a canvas.
Things a geologist carries in the field.Baton: A baton is a conductor's tool. Geologists have hammers, not music, in their kit.

Marvel superheroes.Iron Man: Tony Stark's armored hero debuted in 1963, and the 2008 film launched the Marvel Cinematic Universe.
Marvel superheroes.Thor: Marvel's Thor draws on the Norse god of thunder, and his hammer Mjolnir is named from Old Norse.
Marvel superheroes.Hulk: Bruce Banner's alter ego debuted in 1962. Creator Stan Lee drew inspiration from Jekyll and Hyde, and Frankenstein.
Marvel superheroes.Black Widow: Natasha Romanoff is a former Russian spy who joined the Avengers, and her cinematic solo film arrived in 2021.
Marvel superheroes.Spider-Man: Spider-Man debuted in 1962 and is a teenager under the mask, a novelty for superheroes at the time.
Marvel superheroes.Captain America: Steve Rogers debuted in 1941, and the first cover shows him punching Hitler, almost a year before the US joined WWII.
Marvel superheroes.Black Panther: T'Challa debuted in 1966, before the Black Panther Party was founded. He rules the fictional African nation of Wakanda.
Marvel superheroes.Doctor Strange: Stephen Strange is a former surgeon turned sorcerer, debuting in 1963. His cloak of levitation is a character itself.
Marvel superheroes.Wolverine: Wolverine is a mutant with claws and healing, who debuted in 1974 and became an X-Men favorite.
Marvel superheroes.Deadpool: Deadpool talks to the audience, breaking the fourth wall. He is the merc with a mouth, unlike most Marvel heroes.
Marvel superheroes.Ant-Man: Ant-Man shrinks to insect size. Hank Pym debuted in 1962, and later Scott Lang took the suit in the films.
Marvel superheroes.Batman: Batman belongs to DC Comics, Marvel's biggest rival, and debuted in 1939. He has no superpowers, only wealth and training.
Marvel superheroes.Superman: Superman is a DC hero from 1938, often credited with launching the superhero genre.
Marvel superheroes.Wonder Woman: Wonder Woman is a DC hero, created in 1941 by William Moulton Marston, who also helped develop the polygraph.
Marvel superheroes.Aquaman: Aquaman is DC's king of Atlantis, and a 2018 film of him earned over a billion dollars worldwide.
Marvel superheroes.The Flash: The Flash is a DC speedster. Marvel's own speedster is Quicksilver, and the two are sometimes confused.
Marvel superheroes.Green Lantern: Green Lantern is DC's ring-wielding hero. His power ring is fueled by willpower.
Marvel superheroes.Cyborg: Cyborg is a DC hero and member of the Justice League. He's half human, half machine, no Marvel character.
Marvel superheroes.Supergirl: Supergirl, Superman's cousin Kara, is a DC hero. She debuted in 1959.
Marvel superheroes.Shazam: Shazam was originally called Captain Marvel and belongs to DC, which causes a famous naming mix-up with Marvel.
Marvel superheroes.Robin: Robin is Batman's sidekick, a DC character. He was introduced in 1940 to give Batman someone to talk to.
Marvel superheroes.Batgirl: Batgirl is a DC character, and Barbara Gordon is the best-known one. The 1960s TV show helped introduce her.
Marvel superheroes.Green Arrow: Green Arrow is a DC archer, and Oliver Queen is a billionaire. He's often compared to Batman.
Marvel superheroes.Hawkman: Hawkman is a DC hero with wings and a mace. He's tied to an ancient Egyptian prince's reincarnation.

Russian composers.Tchaikovsky: His 1812 Overture calls for real cannon fire. The Nutcracker, which he wrote near the end of his life, is now a Christmas fixture.
Russian composers.Rachmaninoff: His enormous hands could reportedly stretch a thirteenth on the piano. He left Russia after the 1917 revolution and never returned.
Russian composers.Stravinsky: The 1913 Paris premiere of The Rite of Spring provoked such an uproar in the audience that it is remembered as a near riot.
Russian composers.Prokofiev: He wrote Peter and the Wolf to teach children the instruments of the orchestra, and died on the same day as Stalin, in 1953.
Russian composers.Shostakovich: After Stalin condemned his opera, his Fifth Symphony was hailed as a Soviet artist's reply. Its true meaning is still debated.
Russian composers.Rimsky-Korsakov: A former naval officer who wrote Flight of the Bumblebee and taught Stravinsky, he was a master of orchestration.
Russian composers.Mussorgsky: His piano suite Pictures at an Exhibition is best known in Ravel's orchestral version.
Russian composers.Borodin: A chemist by day, he composed Prince Igor. The musical Kismet later turned his themes into the song Stranger in Paradise.
Russian composers.Glinka: Often called the father of Russian classical music, his 1836 opera A Life for the Tsar launched a national style.
Russian composers.Scriabin: A mystic who linked notes to colors, he included a part for a 'color organ' in his orchestral work Prometheus.
Russian composers.Chopin: Polish, not Russian. He spent his adult life in Paris, and his heart is kept in a church in Warsaw.
Russian composers.Dvořák: Czech, not Russian. He wrote his New World Symphony while directing a conservatory in New York.
Russian composers.Liszt: Hungarian, though he toured Russia in the 1840s to wild acclaim.
Russian composers.Sibelius: A tricky one: he's Finnish, but Finland was ruled by Russia when he composed Finlandia, which was disguised under other titles to dodge censors.
Russian composers.Grieg: Norwegian, famous for the Peer Gynt suite, and a close musical neighbor of Russia only on the map.
Russian composers.Bartók: Hungarian, he recorded and collected thousands of folk melodies across Eastern Europe.
Russian composers.Smetana: Czech, and best known for Vltava, the river piece in his cycle Má vlast.
Russian composers.Brahms: German, from Hamburg. He took over two decades to finish his first symphony.
Russian composers.Wagner: German, and not Russian, though his operas influenced composers everywhere.
Russian composers.Ravel: French, though he orchestrated Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition, which makes him a tempting wrong answer.
Russian composers.Debussy: French. He once visited Russia as a young man, but his Impressionist style is thoroughly Parisian.
Russian composers.Elgar: English, famed for Pomp and Circumstance, and the Enigma Variations that hide a famous unsolved puzzle.
Russian composers.Holst: English, despite his Swedish-sounding name. His suite The Planets omits Earth, and Pluto was undiscovered.
Russian composers.Verdi: Italian, so no. His 1871 Aida premiered in Cairo, not Russia.

Composers from Germany or Austria.Bach: German, born in Eisenach, in a family that produced dozens of musicians in Thuringia.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Beethoven: Born in Bonn, he made his career in Vienna and kept composing after he went deaf.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Mozart: Born in Salzburg, he wrote over 600 works in a life of just 35 years.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Brahms: A Hamburg native who settled in Vienna, which is why he fits both sides of this round.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Wagner: Born in Leipzig, he built a purpose-made opera house at Bayreuth for his own works.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Haydn: Austrian, born in Rohrau. His melody for Austria's old anthem was later reused for Germany's national anthem.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Schubert: A Vienna native who died at 31 after writing about 600 songs and the Unfinished Symphony.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Mahler: Born in Bohemia within the Austrian Empire, he led Vienna's Court Opera, which makes him Austrian by career and culture.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Schumann: German, from Zwickau. His wife Clara was one of the great piano virtuosos of the 19th century.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Mendelssohn: Born in Hamburg, he revived Bach's St Matthew Passion in 1829, which helped spark the Bach revival.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Bruckner: An Austrian organist who wrote nine monumental symphonies and kept revising them for decades.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Chopin: Polish, born near Warsaw. He spent his adult life in France.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Vivaldi: A Venetian, so Italian. He wrote more than 500 concertos.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Verdi: Italian, born in a village near Parma and a hero of Italy's unification.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Puccini: Italian, from Lucca, with a family line of church musicians stretching back generations.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Tchaikovsky: Russian, born in Votkinsk. His ballets became the backbone of classical dance.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Debussy: French. His Clair de lune is among the most loved piano pieces.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Ravel: French, born in the Basque country near Spain. He wrote Boléro.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Grieg: Norwegian, a master of miniature piano pieces and the Peer Gynt suite.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Elgar: English, famous for Pomp and Circumstance and the Enigma Variations.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Rossini: Italian. He stopped writing operas at about 37 and became famed as a gourmet.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Dvořák: Czech. Bohemia was part of the Austrian Empire then, but he is Czech, which makes this a classic trap.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Sibelius: Finnish, and his Finlandia became an unofficial anthem of Finland.
Composers from Germany or Austria.Gershwin: American, from Brooklyn. He wrote Rhapsody in Blue in about three weeks.

ABBA songs.Dancing Queen: ABBA's only US number one. It was premiered at a gala the night before Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf married in 1976.
ABBA songs.Waterloo: It won the 1974 Eurovision Song Contest in Brighton and launched ABBA worldwide, after Sweden's first win.
ABBA songs.Mamma Mia: The song was a hit in 1975, and 24 years later its title became a smash stage musical built around ABBA's songs.
ABBA songs.Fernando: Frida first recorded it in Swedish on her solo album. The English version became a worldwide hit.
ABBA songs.Chiquitita: Performed at a UNICEF benefit concert in 1979, with the royalties donated to the charity.
ABBA songs.Take a Chance on Me: Björn reportedly got the rhythm from the sound of his own steps while jogging, hence the unusual chant-like backing.
ABBA songs.SOS: John Lennon reportedly named it among his favorite songs of the time, and it was a rare comeback for a pop group.
ABBA songs.Super Trouper: Named after a powerful spotlight used on stage, and it gave its name to the 1980 album.
ABBA songs.Gimme! Gimme! Gimme!: Subtitled A Man After Midnight, its riff was sampled by Madonna on Hung Up in 2005.
ABBA songs.Money Money Money: A cabaret-flavored tune about wanting riches, from the 1976 album Arrival. Its dramatic style drew on the musical Cabaret.
ABBA songs.Voulez-Vous: French for do you want, it was partly recorded at Criteria Studios in Miami in 1979, with a disco beat.
ABBA songs.I Will Survive: Gloria Gaynor's 1978 disco anthem, not ABBA's, though it was recorded in the same disco era.
ABBA songs.Like a Prayer: Madonna's 1989 song, famous for its controversial video that cost her a Pepsi sponsorship.
ABBA songs.Rasputin: Boney M's disco take on the Russian mystic, not ABBA, though ABBA had their own Russian-tinged feel on Eagle.
ABBA songs.Daddy Cool: A 1976 hit by Boney M, a studio-assembled disco group, so not ABBA, though the sounds are similar.
ABBA songs.Rivers of Babylon: Boney M's 1978 hit, and an adaptation of a Jamaican reggae tune, with lyrics from Psalms.
ABBA songs.YMCA: Village People's 1978 hit, with the famous letter-spelling arm dance that fans still do at weddings.
ABBA songs.Hot Stuff: Donna Summer's 1979 disco rocker, with a rock guitar solo, and it's not ABBA.
ABBA songs.Le Freak: Chic's 1978 disco classic, reportedly born after the band was refused entry to Studio 54.
ABBA songs.Waterloo Sunset: The Kinks' 1967 ode to London, a trap next to ABBA's Waterloo, though the two are entirely unrelated.
ABBA songs.Dancing in the Dark: Bruce Springsteen's 1984 hit, not Dancing Queen, and its video featured a young Courteney Cox.
ABBA songs.Hey Jude: A Beatles hit from 1968, a seven-minute song, and no relation to ABBA at all.
ABBA songs.Heart of Glass: Blondie's 1979 disco-rock hit, from the album Parallel Lines, and not by ABBA.
ABBA songs.Super Freak: Rick James's 1981 funk hit, and its bass riff was sampled in U Can't Touch This.

Famous ballets.Swan Lake: Tchaikovsky's first ballet flopped at its 1877 Moscow premiere; the 1895 revival in St Petersburg made it the icon, with one dancer playing both Odette and Odile.
Famous ballets.The Nutcracker: Tchaikovsky's 1892 score bombed at first, yet this Christmas ballet now brings many companies a huge share of their yearly ticket sales.
Famous ballets.Giselle: Premiered in Paris in 1841, this ghostly Romantic ballet has a peasant girl die of heartbreak, then save her betrayer from vengeful spirits.
Famous ballets.Coppélia: A comic ballet from 1870 about a young man who falls for a life-size doll, mistaking her for a real girl. Comedies are rare in ballet.
Famous ballets.The Rite of Spring: Stravinsky's 1913 score and Nijinsky's jarring choreography so shocked a Paris audience that the premiere is remembered as a near riot.
Famous ballets.The Firebird: Stravinsky was only 28 when this 1910 ballet, based on Russian folk tales, made him famous overnight. It was his first score for Diaghilev.
Famous ballets.La Bayadère: This 1877 Petipa ballet is set in India. Its Kingdom of the Shades scene has dancers filing down a ramp in an endless line of white tutus.
Famous ballets.Sleeping Beauty: Tchaikovsky's 1890 ballet gave Disney the waltz it later reused for Once Upon a Dream in the 1959 animated film.
Famous ballets.Don Quixote: Only a slice of Cervantes's novel is told here, and the story is mostly about the lovers Kitri and Basilio, not the windmill-tilting knight.
Famous ballets.Romeo and Juliet: Prokofiev's 1930s score opens the famous Dance of the Knights, a thundering theme you have likely heard in films and TV.
Famous ballets.Aida: Verdi's opera, set in ancient Egypt, premiered in Cairo in 1871. It does include a ballet in its triumphal scene, but it is sung, not danced.
Famous ballets.Tosca: Puccini's 1900 opera ends with the heroine leaping from Rome's Castel Sant'Angelo. It is an opera through and through.
Famous ballets.La Bohème: Puccini's tale of artists in Paris premiered in 1896 and later inspired the musical Rent. Sung, not danced.
Famous ballets.Madama Butterfly: Puccini's opera about a geisha in Nagasaki flopped at La Scala in 1904, so he revised it and it became a classic.
Famous ballets.Magic Flute: Mozart's last opera premiered in 1791, just weeks before his death. The Queen of the Night's aria is a famous test for sopranos.
Famous ballets.Fidelio: Beethoven's only opera, which he rewrote several times over about a decade. A rescue story, entirely sung.
Famous ballets.Turandot: Puccini died in 1924 before finishing it, and Nessun dorma comes from this opera. No ballet here.
Famous ballets.Rigoletto: Verdi reportedly kept La donna e mobile secret until just before the 1851 premiere so it would not leak. An opera, not a ballet.
Famous ballets.The Four Seasons: Vivaldi's four violin concertos paint spring, summer, autumn and winter in sound. Choreographers have danced to them, but it is not a ballet.
Famous ballets.The Planets: Holst's suite has seven movements, one per planet except Earth, and was finished before Pluto was discovered. Orchestral, not a ballet.
Famous ballets.Messiah: Handel wrote this oratorio in about three weeks in 1741. Audiences traditionally stand for the Hallelujah chorus.
Famous ballets.Moonlight Sonata: The Moonlight nickname came from a critic after Beethoven's death, not from him. A piano sonata, not a ballet.
Famous ballets.New World Symphony: Dvorak wrote this symphony in the USA in 1893, and Neil Armstrong reportedly took a recording to the Moon. It is not a ballet.
Famous ballets.Requiem: A mass for the dead. Mozart left his unfinished when he died in 1791, and his pupil Sussmayr completed it.

Things that ring.Telephone: Alexander Graham Bell's 1876 invention rang bells at first, and later mechanical ringers were replaced by electronic tones.
Things that ring.Doorbell: The electric doorbell was invented in 1831 by American scientist Joseph Henry, who also built early electromagnets.
Things that ring.Church bell: Some towers swing them through full circles in change ringing, a British tradition with elaborate patterns.
Things that ring.Bicycle bell: Many places, including the UK, require new bikes sold to have a bell, a small safety device with a cheerful ding.
Things that ring.School bell: A time-honoured signal for classes, once rung by hand, and now usually electric.
Things that ring.Alarm clock: Levi Hutchins of New Hampshire built one in 1787, but it only rang at 4 a.m., his waking time.
Things that ring.Boxing bell: Ding ding starts each round, and the phrase saved by the bell is thought to come from boxing.
Things that ring.Handbell: English bell ringers developed these for practising tower bell changes, and handbell choirs followed.
Things that ring.Tuning fork: Invented in 1711 by John Shore, a trumpeter, it vibrates at one pure pitch, and its A rings at 440 Hz.
Things that ring.Car horn: It honks or toots, and does not ring, though some old cars used bells.
Things that ring.Whistle: A whistle blows or shrills, and does not ring, as air is forced through a small gap.
Things that ring.Siren: It wails, and its name comes from the Sirens of Greek myth, who lured sailors with song.
Things that ring.Snare drum: It is struck, not rung, and gives a dry thump or crack, though its snares buzz.
Things that ring.Kazoo: It buzzes, rather than rings, as its membrane vibrates.
Things that ring.Thunder: It rumbles or rolls, and does not ring like a bell. The sound comes from air heated by lightning.
Things that ring.Bagpipes: It skirls with a reedy drone, and does not ring.
Things that ring.Rattle: It rattles with a dry shake, and does not ring.
Things that ring.Foghorn: A foghorn sounds a low blast, not a ring, and was invented to warn ships.
Things that ring.Vuvuzela: It drones with a loud, monotonous blare, and became famous at the 2010 World Cup.
Things that ring.Tuba: A tuba oompahs with a deep brass sound, not a ring.
Things that ring.Hiccup: A hiccup is a sudden contraction, with a short, sharp sound, and does not ring.
Things that ring.Sneeze: A sneeze can reach speeds of about 100 miles per hour, but it does not ring.
Things that ring.Guitar: Chords on a guitar can ring out as strings vibrate freely, but the instrument is strummed, not rung.
Things that ring.Maracas: Shaken, so it rattles, with a dry, rhythmic sound rather than a ring.

Christmas songs.Jingle Bells: Written in the 1850s for Thanksgiving, it was reportedly the first song broadcast from space, by Gemini 6 astronauts in 1965.
Christmas songs.Silent Night: First sung in 1818 in an Austrian church, reportedly with a guitar because the organ was broken; it is now sung worldwide.
Christmas songs.White Christmas: Irving Berlin's 1942 song is widely cited as the best-selling single of all time, with Bing Crosby's version above 50 million copies.
Christmas songs.Feliz Navidad: José Feliciano wrote it in 1970, and its lyric is only a Spanish greeting and an English line, making it easy for everyone to sing.
Christmas songs.Last Christmas: Wham!'s 1984 hit was kept off the UK number one spot by Band Aid's charity single that Christmas, and it has returned to the charts almost every December since.
Christmas songs.Deck the Halls: Its tune is from a 16th-century Welsh song, 'Nos Galan', and the English words came from the 1800s.
Christmas songs.Frosty the Snowman: Written in 1950 as a follow-up to 'Rudolph', it tells of a snowman who comes alive because of a magic silk hat.
Christmas songs.Little Drummer Boy: Katherine Davis wrote it in 1941 as 'Carol of the Drum', and its steady rum-pum-pum-pum imitates a drum beat.
Christmas songs.Joy to the World: Isaac Watts wrote it in 1719, based on Psalm 98, and it is often cited as the most-published Christmas hymn in North America.
Christmas songs.O Holy Night: This French carol of 1847 was among the first pieces ever broadcast on radio, on Christmas Eve 1906.

Things that squeak.Mouse: High-pitched squeaks are only part of it; male mice also sing ultrasonic songs to attract mates that we can't hear.
Things that squeak.Door hinge: Squeaks come from friction, the hinge sticking and slipping against its pin hundreds of times a second.
Things that squeak.Guinea pig: Guinea pigs 'wheek' loudly, famously at the sound of a fridge door or approaching food.
Things that squeak.Dog toy: The squeaker inside is likely so popular because the sound mimics prey, which can trigger a dog's hunting instinct.
Things that squeak.Rubber duck: In 1992, thousands of bath toys fell off a ship in the Pacific and drifted for years, helping scientists study ocean currents.
Things that squeak.Floorboard: Floorboards squeak when nails or edges rub; a dusting of talcum powder between them is a common fix.
Things that squeak.Brakes: Brake squeal comes from vibration between pad and rotor, often caused by dust, glazing or worn pads.
Things that squeak.Hamster: Hamsters carry food in stretchy cheek pouches that reach back toward their hips, and they squeak when upset.
Things that squeak.Sneakers: Sneakers got their name because rubber soles let wearers sneak up quietly, until they hit a gym floor.
Things that squeak.Lion: Lions roar, a sound that can carry up to about eight kilometres across the savanna.
Things that squeak.Cow: Cows moo, and the idea that they have four stomachs is a myth: it's one stomach with four chambers.
Things that squeak.Thunder: Thunder rumbles; the sound comes from air superheated by lightning, so it's no squeak.
Things that squeak.Drum: Drums boom and thump, and the pitch depends on how tight the head is.
Things that squeak.Owl: Owls hoot, and their fringed feathers make flight near-silent, so squeaking isn't their thing.
Things that squeak.Wolf: Wolves howl, a call that can carry for kilometres and help a pack find its members.
Things that squeak.Elephant: Elephants trumpet and rumble, communicating partly in infrasound too low for people to hear.
Things that squeak.Church bell: A church bell peals with deep tones, far from a squeak, and a big one can weigh many tonnes.
Things that squeak.Bass guitar: A bass guitar thumps with very low frequencies, usually from four thick strings.
Things that squeak.Waterfall: Waterfalls roar from constantly crashing water, a sound audible from far away.
Things that squeak.Lawnmower: Lawnmowers whir and drone, and the first one was patented in 1830 in England.
Things that squeak.Tuba: The tuba plays the lowest notes of the brass family, and the tuba's deep sound is the opposite of a squeak.
Things that squeak.Horse: Horses neigh and whinny, calls that can carry across fields.
Things that squeak.Frog: Frogs croak, and the Hollywood 'ribbit' comes from the Pacific tree frog.
Things that squeak.Bear: Bears growl, huff and moan, and a squeak doesn't suit them.

Motown artists.Stevie Wonder: Signed to Motown at eleven and blind from infancy, he has won 25 Grammys. His 1970s run of albums is legendary.

Motown artists.The Temptations: Known for their sharp choreography and five-man harmony, they sang My Girl, written by Smokey Robinson. They've had many lineup changes.
Motown artists.Smokey Robinson: As leader of the Miracles and a prolific songwriter, he also served as a Motown vice president. Bob Dylan called him America's greatest living poet.
Motown artists.Jackson 5: Motown signed the family group in 1968, and their first four singles went to number one. Michael was only about ten when they started.
Motown artists.Diana Ross: She left the Supremes in 1970 and became a solo star and actress. She was nominated for an Oscar for playing Billie Holiday in Lady Sings the Blues.
Motown artists.The Four Tops: Their classic lineup stayed together for over four decades without changes. Reach Out I'll Be There was a 1966 hit.
Motown artists.Lionel Richie: He started with the Commodores and then became a solo superstar. His 1983 album Can't Slow Down sold over 20 million copies.
Motown artists.The Commodores: Funk and soul group from Tuskegee, Alabama, with Lionel Richie. Their hits included Easy and Three Times a Lady.
Motown artists.Mary Wells: Motown's first female star, with My Guy in 1964. She left the label soon after, a move many see as hurting her career.
Motown artists.Aretha Franklin: The Queen of Soul recorded for Columbia and then Atlantic. Respect, her best-known song, was originally an Otis Redding track.
Motown artists.Otis Redding: Stax Records, in Memphis, was his label, a southern rival to Motown. He died in a plane crash in 1967 at age 26.
Motown artists.James Brown: The Godfather of Soul recorded for King Records and Polydor, not Motown. His rhythmic emphasis on the first beat helped create funk.
Motown artists.Ray Charles: He recorded for Atlantic, then ABC-Paramount, and not for Motown. His 1962 country album was a big surprise at the time.
Motown artists.Sam Cooke: He was a gospel star turned pop star for RCA, and founded his own label SAR. He died in 1964, aged 33.
Motown artists.Elvis Presley: The King recorded first at Sun Records in Memphis and then RCA. Motown, based in Detroit, was a very different sound.
Motown artists.Whitney Houston: She was signed to Arista Records by Clive Davis, not Motown. Her 1992 version of I Will Always Love You was a record-breaking hit.
Motown artists.Prince: The Minneapolis artist recorded for Warner Bros., and he is from the Minneapolis Sound world, not Detroit.
Motown artists.Tina Turner: Her early hits were on Sue and later Capitol labels, not Motown. Her 1984 album Private Dancer made her a solo star at 44.
Motown artists.Al Green: Soul singer who made his best records at Hi Records in Memphis. Hi's silky sound was distinct from Motown's Detroit style.
Motown artists.Wilson Pickett: He recorded Midnight Hour and 634-5789 for Atlantic and Stax. His gritty Southern soul was a contrast to Motown polish.
Motown artists.Etta James: At Last was recorded for Chess Records in Chicago. She was one of that label's great blues and soul voices.
Motown artists.Johnny Cash: Cash recorded for Sun, Columbia and American Recordings. He is a country figure, far from Detroit's soul sound.

Beatles albums.Please Please Me: Their 1963 debut was recorded mostly in a single day, in about 10 hours at Abbey Road. It rushed out quickly.
Beatles albums.With the Beatles: Their 1963 second album, with a moody black and white cover. Its photographer was Robert Freeman.
Beatles albums.A Hard Day's Night: Their 1964 album was the first to contain only Lennon-McCartney originals. It's also a film soundtrack.
Beatles albums.Magical Mystery Tour: The 1967 release accompanied a TV film. In the US, it was issued as a full album, unlike in the UK.
Beatles albums.Beatles for Sale: Their 1964 album has a tired, weary cover shot and includes several covers among the originals, a sign of the busy touring schedule.
Beatles albums.Pet Sounds: A 1966 Beach Boys album by Brian Wilson. It was in part a response to Rubber Soul and inspired Sgt. Pepper.

Beatles albums.Imagine: John Lennon's 1971 solo album. Its title song is among the most famous peace anthems.

Beatles albums.Blonde on Blonde: Dylan's 1966 double album, widely credited as rock's first double studio album. It is not by the Beatles.

Beatles albums.Sticky Fingers: The Stones' 1971 album had a zippered jeans cover by Andy Warhol. It's by the Rolling Stones.
Beatles albums.Who's Next: The Who's 1971 album uses synthesizers on Baba O'Riley. It is not a Beatles album.
Beatles albums.Thriller: Michael Jackson's 1982 album is the best-selling of all time. It isn't by the Beatles.

Words that rhyme with 'song'.Wrong: Comes from Old Norse rangr, meaning crooked or twisted.

Words that rhyme with 'song'.Gong: Imitates a sound; the word reached English via Malay, and gamelan orchestras are built around gongs.
Words that rhyme with 'song'.Ping-pong: A trademark name of Parker Brothers for table tennis; US and China swapped teams in 1971's ping-pong diplomacy.
Words that rhyme with 'song'.Throng: Also a verb meaning to crowd into a place: people throng the streets.
Words that rhyme with 'song'.Belong: From Middle English belongen, 'to go along with'; the 'long' in belong has nothing to do with length.
Words that rhyme with 'song'.Along: From Old English andlang, which means 'against the length' of something.
Words that rhyme with 'song'.Prolong: Pro plus Latin longus, 'long': to prolong is to make longer.
Words that rhyme with 'song'.King Kong: The 1933 film's giant ape climbs the Empire State Building; the sequel Son of Kong came the same year.
Words that rhyme with 'song'.Sarong: A word borrowed from Malay for a wraparound garment, worn in Southeast Asia and Pacific.
Words that rhyme with 'song'.Oolong: From Chinese wulong, 'black dragon'; this tea is partly oxidized, between green and black.
Words that rhyme with 'song'.Sung: Sung is spelled like song but rhymes with tongue; it is the past participle of sing, as in 'she has sung'.

Words that rhyme with 'song'.Tongue: Tongue ends in -ongue like gong, but is pronounced 'tung'; English spelling hides many such traps.
Words that rhyme with 'song'.Young: Young looks like it should rhyme with long, but it rhymes with sung; both come from Old English geong.

Words that rhyme with 'song'.Hung: Hung is spelled like it would rhyme with song, but it takes the short u and rhymes with sung and young.
