In 'My Favorite Things'.Raindrops on roses: The song from "The Sound of Music" opens with this line, and it was written by Rodgers and Hammerstein in 1959.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Whiskers on kittens: The second line of the song, and Julie Andrews sang it in the 1965 film, which won five Oscars.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Copper kettles: Copper conducts heat extremely well, and kettles made of it heat water faster than steel ones.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Warm woolen mittens: Mittens keep fingers warmer than gloves because the fingers share warmth, and the line is spelt "woolen" in the lyrics.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Brown paper packages: The line goes "tied up with strings", and the phrase has become a Christmas image though the original song is not about Christmas.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Crisp apple strudels: Strudel is a pastry from Austria, where the musical is set, and its dough is stretched so thin you can see through it.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Doorbells: The song lists "doorbells and sleigh bells and schnitzel with noodles", an Austrian touch.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Sleigh bells: They appear right alongside doorbells in the lyrics, and the song is a popular Christmas standard despite not being about Christmas.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Schnitzel: It appears in the line "schnitzel with noodles", and wiener schnitzel is a breaded veal cutlet that is Austria's national dish.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Wild geese: The line "wild geese that fly with the moon on their wings" is among the song's most poetic images.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Snowflakes: "Snowflakes that stay on my nose and eyelashes" is the line, and no two snowflakes are said to be alike.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Silver white winters: The line is "silver white winters that melt into springs", and the lyric ends the verse with a change in season.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Ponies: "Cream-colored ponies" are in the song's second line, and they're often forgotten in favour of the flashier things.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Puppies: The song has kittens, not puppies, so this one is often mixed up with another song.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Ice cream: It's not in the song, and ice cream is more associated with other tunes.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Rainbows: They're in "Over the Rainbow" from "The Wizard of Oz", not in this song.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Sunshine: Not in the lyrics, which stick to wintery images such as snowflakes.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Lollipops: It's from a different song, and lollipops are in "The Good Ship Lollipop".
In 'My Favorite Things'.Butterflies: They aren't listed, and the song's creatures are kittens, geese, and ponies.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Teddy bears: They are not named in the lyrics, which feature kittens as the cuddly creature.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Candy canes: They are not in the song, though it's often played at Christmas, and the lyrics don't mention sweets beyond strudel.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Fireworks: Not in the lyric, which goes for quieter wintery things.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Cupcakes: They are not in the song, and apple strudel is the only pastry on its list.
In 'My Favorite Things'.Bubbles: Not in the song, which lists things like snowflakes and kettles instead.

Real people of the Wild West.Billy the Kid: Born Henry McCarty, he was killed at about 21 by Sheriff Pat Garrett in 1881 in New Mexico.
Real people of the Wild West.Jesse James: The outlaw robbed banks and trains, and was shot in the back in 1882 by Robert Ford, a gang member seeking the reward.
Real people of the Wild West.Wyatt Earp: The lawman fought in the 1881 O.K. Corral shootout, which lasted only about 30 seconds.
Real people of the Wild West.Doc Holliday: A dentist turned gambler, he had tuberculosis and died in bed in 1887, aged 36.
Real people of the Wild West.Wild Bill Hickok: He was shot dead in 1876 while playing poker in Deadwood, holding aces and eights, now known as the dead man's hand.
Real people of the Wild West.Calamity Jane: Born Martha Jane Cannary, she was a scout and storyteller who asked to be buried next to Hickok in Deadwood.
Real people of the Wild West.Annie Oakley: A sharpshooter in Buffalo Bill's show, she shot playing cards edge-on, and the holes inspired the term 'Annie Oakley' for a free ticket.
Real people of the Wild West.Buffalo Bill: William Cody turned himself into a legend with a Wild West show that toured Europe and performed for Queen Victoria.
Real people of the Wild West.Butch Cassidy: Born Robert LeRoy Parker, he led the Wild Bunch gang, and his fate in Bolivia in the early 1900s is still debated.
Real people of the Wild West.Sundance Kid: Harry Longabaugh took his nickname from Sundance, Wyoming, where he was once jailed for stealing a horse.
Real people of the Wild West.Sitting Bull: A Lakota leader who helped win the Little Bighorn in 1876, he later briefly toured with Buffalo Bill's show.
Real people of the Wild West.Belle Starr: Called the Bandit Queen, she lived in Oklahoma Indian Territory and was shot dead in 1889; dime novels inflated her legend.
Real people of the Wild West.Lone Ranger: Fictional: he began in a 1933 radio show, and the masked rider's silver bullets are made up.
Real people of the Wild West.Zorro: Johnston McCulley invented him in 1919, set in Spanish California, and he's fiction, not history.
Real people of the Wild West.Rooster Cogburn: Charles Portis created him in True Grit, and John Wayne won his only Oscar playing the eye-patched marshal.
Real people of the Wild West.Django: The coffin-dragging gunslinger is from Sergio Corbucci's 1966 spaghetti western, not real history.
Real people of the Wild West.Tonto: The Lone Ranger's sidekick is fictional, and his portrayal, mostly in broken English, is now widely criticized.
Real people of the Wild West.Hopalong Cassidy: A fictional cowboy hero from Clarence Mulford's stories who became an early TV star in the 1950s.
Real people of the Wild West.Clint Eastwood: He's a real actor born in 1930, famous for playing westerners but not one himself.
Real people of the Wild West.John Wayne: Real, and he played cowboys, but he was born in 1907 in Iowa, long after the Wild West era.
Real people of the Wild West.Paul Revere: He belongs to the American Revolution: his famous ride was in 1775, and the West was still unsettled.
Real people of the Wild West.Pecos Bill: A tall-tale cowboy invented in print in the early 1900s who supposedly rode a cyclone.
Real people of the Wild West.Yosemite Sam: The Looney Tunes loudmouth first appeared in 1945 as a Bugs Bunny foe.
Real people of the Wild West.Marshal Dillon: Fictional lawman of the Gunsmoke radio and TV series set in Dodge City, Kansas.

Historic walls.Hadrian's Wall: Built from AD 122 across northern England, it marked the edge of Roman Britain and had a fort every few miles along its length of about 73 miles.
Historic walls.Great Wall of China: Many walls built across dynasties make up its network, and contrary to a popular myth, it is not visible to the naked eye from the Moon.
Historic walls.Berlin Wall: It split the German city from 1961 until November 1989, and it was the Cold War's most famous barrier. It fell after border rules were suddenly relaxed.
Historic walls.Antonine Wall: Romans built this turf wall across Scotland around AD 142, north of Hadrian's Wall, but abandoned it after about 20 years.
Historic walls.Theodosian Walls: Constantinople's massive triple land walls, built in the 5th century, protected the city for around a thousand years until Ottoman cannons broke them in 1453.
Historic walls.Western Wall: A remnant of the retaining wall of the Second Temple's platform in Jerusalem, it is a sacred place where people tuck prayer notes into the cracks.
Historic walls.Aurelian Walls: Rome built these defenses in the 270s AD, and much of their 19 km circuit still stands today, with gates still in use.
Historic walls.Servian Wall: Older than Aurelian's, this early Roman wall was traditionally credited to King Servius Tullius, though it dates from the 4th century BC. Pieces survive near Termini station.
Historic walls.Walls of Dubrovnik: These medieval walls ring the Croatian old town and are walkable for about two kilometres. They also featured as King's Landing in Game of Thrones.
Historic walls.Walls of Avila: This Spanish city boasts some of Europe's best-preserved medieval walls, with some 2,500 towers and a stone circuit of about 2.5 km.
Historic walls.Wall Street: Trap: the name does recall a real wall, a wooden stockade built by Dutch settlers in the 1600s in what became New York, but the wall is long gone.
Historic walls.Great Barrier Reef: Trap: a 'barrier' of living coral off Queensland, not a built wall. It stretches over 2,000 km and is the largest living structure on Earth.
Historic walls.Golden Gate Bridge: Trap: this is a bridge, completed in 1937, whose famous color is officially called International Orange, not gold.
Historic walls.Stonehenge: Trap: a ring of standing stones in England, raised about 4,500 years ago. It is a monument, not a defensive wall.
Historic walls.Brandenburg Gate: Trap: though tied to the Berlin Wall's story, since the Wall ran just beside it, it is an 18th-century neoclassical gateway, not a wall.
Historic walls.Arc de Triomphe: Trap: Napoleon ordered this Paris triumphal arch in 1806 to honor his army, and it was only finished in the 1830s. An arch, not a wall.
Historic walls.Colosseum: Trap: Rome's great amphitheatre, opened in AD 80, could hold tens of thousands of spectators. Its outer wall is impressive, but it is not a city wall.
Historic walls.Hoover Dam: Trap: a huge concrete wall, yes, but it holds back a river, not an enemy. It was built on the Colorado River in the 1930s.
Historic walls.Panama Canal: Trap: it is a waterway connecting two oceans, opened in 1914, so no wall here.
Historic walls.Tower of Pisa: Trap: it leans because it was built on soft ground, and began tilting before it was even finished. It is a bell tower, not a wall.
Historic walls.Sphinx: Trap: the Great Sphinx at Giza is a statue with a lion's body, carved from limestone bedrock around 4,500 years ago.
Historic walls.Rubicon: Trap: a small river in northern Italy that Julius Caesar crossed in 49 BC, starting a civil war. 'Crossing the Rubicon' means a point of no return.
Historic walls.Suez Canal: Trap: an Egyptian waterway opened in 1869 that links the Mediterranean and Red seas and spares ships a trip around Africa.
Historic walls.Wallace Monument: Trap: sounds wall-like, but it is a tower near Stirling, Scotland, honoring William Wallace, completed in 1869.

Things you'd find in a bathroom.Towel: Terry cloth towels hold water in thousands of tiny loops, and the fabric's looped pile is what makes it absorbent.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Shampoo: The word comes from the Hindi 'champo', meaning to massage, and was brought to Britain from India in the 1800s.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Bath mat: Cotton or rubber, it soaks up drips and grips wet tile. Falls in the bathroom are among the most common household injuries.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Toilet paper: Chinese records mention it by the 6th century, and the first commercial rolls in the US appeared in 1857.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Loofah: Despite the sea-sponge look, it comes from the dried fibrous insides of a gourd plant that grows like a cucumber.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Shower curtain: The first appeared around the 1900s as showers entered homes, and a clinging curtain is explained by air pressure from the moving water.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Razor: Ancient people shaved with sharpened flints and shells, and the safety razor with a replaceable blade came from King Gillette in 1901.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Plunger: A simple rubber cup that works by moving water, and in the US the modern plunger design was patented in the 1870s.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Soap dish: A small tray that lets soap drain, and without one, a bar left in water turns to mush.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Mouthwash: Antiseptic rinses date back centuries, and Listerine was named after Joseph Lister, the pioneer of antiseptic surgery.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Dental floss: Dentist Levi Spear Parmly recommended silk thread to clean between teeth in 1815, long before floss became common.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Oven mitt: Trap: a kitchen item that protects hands from hot pans, so it lives by the stove.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Colander: Trap: a bowl with holes for draining pasta, a kitchen item, from Latin for 'to strain'.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Stapler: Trap: an office tool, and early staplers were reportedly made for King Louis XV's court in 18th-century France.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Lawnmower: Trap: invented by Edwin Budding in 1830 in England, for the garden, and it was first used to trim sports grounds.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Toaster: Trap: it lives in the kitchen, and the pop-up toaster was patented in 1919.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Spatula: Trap: a kitchen flipper, and the word comes from the Latin for a flat piece of wood.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Rolling pin: Trap: a baking tool for flattening dough, and it also reappears in cartoons as a weapon.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Hammock: Trap: a hanging bed from the Caribbean, whose name comes from the Taíno word hamaca.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Whisk: Trap: a kitchen tool for beating air into eggs or cream.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Doormat: Trap: it goes at the entrance to wipe shoes, outside rather than in the bathroom.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Wrench: Trap: a workshop tool for turning bolts and nuts, so it belongs in the toolbox, though a plumber might bring one to fix the sink.
Things you'd find in a bathroom.Cheese grater: Trap: a kitchen tool, with sharp holes that shred cheese, and sometimes a nasty grater for hands.

Things with buttons.Remote control: Early TV remotes were wired; Zenith's 1956 Space Command used ultrasound, so jingling keys could change the channel.
Things with buttons.Dress shirt: Men's shirts button right over left and women's left over right, a quirk whose origin historians still debate.
Things with buttons.Calculator: Pocket calculators arrived in the early 1970s; before that, electronic ones were desk-sized machines costing a small fortune.
Things with buttons.Elevator: Elisha Otis demonstrated his safety brake in 1854 by cutting the hoist rope himself, making tall buildings practical.
Things with buttons.Doorbell: Electric doorbells appeared in the 1800s, and many homes still use a push button on low-voltage wiring.
Things with buttons.Microwave: Engineer Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melting near a radar magnetron around 1945, which led to the microwave oven.
Things with buttons.Game controller: Nintendo's Famicom pad popularized the plus-shaped D-pad, designed by Gunpei Yokoi for an earlier Donkey Kong handheld.
Things with buttons.Computer mouse: Douglas Engelbart's 1960s wooden prototype had a single button, and its trailing cord looked like a tail.
Things with buttons.Vending machine: Heron of Alexandria described a coin-operated device dispensing holy water about two thousand years ago.
Things with buttons.Cardigan: It's named for the 7th Earl of Cardigan, a British officer in the Crimean War era, who made the knitted jacket famous.
Things with buttons.Jeans: Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis patented copper rivets for work trousers in 1873, which still reinforce jeans today.
Things with buttons.Banana: No buttons, but a botanical surprise: bananas count as berries, while strawberries do not.
Things with buttons.Sock: Buttonless, but the oldest known knitted socks come from Egypt and are roughly a thousand years old.
Things with buttons.Spoon: Spoons predate forks by millennia; carved ones go back to at least the Stone Age.
Things with buttons.Candle: The base unit of light intensity, the candela, is named for the candle, though it's now defined by a precise light frequency.
Things with buttons.Broom: Shakers are credited with the flat broom, which let people sweep more efficiently, in the early 1800s.
Things with buttons.Hammer: Stone hammering tools go back roughly three million years, long before buttons existed.
Things with buttons.Pencil: 'Lead' is actually graphite mixed with clay, and England's Borrowdale deposit launched the pencil trade in the 1500s.
Things with buttons.Ladder: A ladder's safe angle follows the 4-to-1 rule: one unit out from the wall for every four units of height.
Things with buttons.Plate: US dinner plates have crept larger over decades, one reason portion sizes seem to have grown.
Things with buttons.Fork: A fork reached Western Europe slowly; an 11th-century Byzantine princess's fork in Venice scandalized clergy, the story goes.
Things with buttons.Sponge: A natural sponge is an animal with no organs or brain; most kitchen sponges are synthetic cellulose or foam.
Things with buttons.Towel: Terry cloth's loops multiply surface area, which is why towels soak up so much water.
Things with buttons.Bucket: The idiom 'kick the bucket' has uncertain origins; one theory points to a beam used to hang slaughtered pigs.

Things that rust.Iron nail: Rust forms when iron meets oxygen and water, and the flaky orange layer keeps eating the nail underneath.
Things that rust.Bike chain: A bike chain is steel, and without oil it rusts quickly, especially after riding in rain.
Things that rust.Iron gate: Painted or galvanized iron resists rust, but a scratch exposes the metal and starts the orange creep.
Things that rust.Steel wool: Steel wool is so thin and has so much surface area that a damp pad can rust in a day or two.
Things that rust.Cast iron pan: Seasoning a cast iron pan with baked-on oil makes a barrier, which keeps rust away and the surface slick.
Things that rust.Steel can: Steel cans have a thin coating of tin or plastic, and a dent that cracks it will let rust in.
Things that rust.Anchor: Steel anchors are hot-dip galvanized with zinc, because salt water speeds up rusting dramatically.
Things that rust.Barbed wire: Galvanized barbed wire holds up outdoors, but eventually the zinc wears away and the steel begins to rust.
Things that rust.Iron railings: Railings need repainting every few years, because rust expands as it forms and can crack the paint.
Things that rust.Horseshoe: Horseshoes are steel and rust in damp ground, so the shiny ones sold as souvenirs are usually coated.
Things that rust.Plastic chair: Plastic is a polymer with no iron in it, so it cannot rust, though it can fade or crack in sunlight.
Things that rust.Gold ring: Gold is one of the least reactive metals, which is why ancient gold objects still shine after thousands of years.
Things that rust.Glass bottle: Glass is silica and does not rust, and roman glass can last thousands of years.
Things that rust.Aluminum can: Aluminum forms a thin oxide skin that protects the metal underneath, so it corrodes without ever rusting.
Things that rust.Copper pipe: Copper corrodes into a green patina, like the Statue of Liberty's, but it does not rust.
Things that rust.Wooden fence: Wood rots and splits when it gets wet, but because it contains no iron it cannot rust.
Things that rust.Rubber boot: Rubber does not rust, though over time sunlight and ozone can crack it.
Things that rust.Silver spoon: Silver tarnishes black from sulfur in the air, but it does not rust.
Things that rust.Brick: Brick is fired clay, and a brick red color comes from iron oxide, which is already effectively rust.
Things that rust.Ceramic mug: Ceramic is baked clay with a glaze, and it does not rust.
Things that rust.Paper: Paper yellows and breaks down with age and moisture, but it does not rust.
Things that rust.Candle: A candle's wax and wick contain no iron, so it cannot rust.
Things that rust.Granite: Granite can show orange stains where its iron minerals oxidize, but the stone itself does not rust.
Things that rust.Bronze statue: Bronze is mostly copper and tin, and it develops a green-brown patina instead of rust.

Idioms that mention a body part.Cold feet: Possibly from 19th-century gambling slang, it now means sudden nerves before a big commitment, like a wedding.
Idioms that mention a body part.Break a leg: Theater superstition says wishing 'good luck' invites bad luck, so performers wish each other a broken leg.
Idioms that mention a body part.Elbow grease: Elbow grease means hard physical effort, and it has been used in English since the 1600s.
Idioms that mention a body part.All ears: Said by someone ready to listen closely, as if the whole person were one big ear.
Idioms that mention a body part.Lend a hand: Lend a hand means to help out, and 'a big hand' for applause uses the same body part.
Idioms that mention a body part.Chin up: Chin up is encouragement to keep one's head high in hardship, much like keeping a stiff upper lip.
Idioms that mention a body part.Head over heels: It oddly describes the normal position, since the older form was 'heels over head'.
Idioms that mention a body part.Thumbs up: Popular belief ties it to Roman gladiator crowds, but historians doubt the gesture meant what we think.
Idioms that mention a body part.Heart of gold: Heart of gold means kind and generous; Shakespeare's Henry V uses the phrase.
Idioms that mention a body part.Pain in the neck: A politer cousin of a cruder body-part phrase, it labels someone or something annoying.
Idioms that mention a body part.Tongue-tied: Tongue-tied means speechless, and the medical sense is ankyloglossia, a short band under the tongue.
Idioms that mention a body part.Keep an eye out: It uses just one eye, but means to watch carefully for something.
Idioms that mention a body part.Piece of cake: No body part here; it means very easy, perhaps from cakes awarded as prizes in cakewalk contests.
Idioms that mention a body part.Spill the beans: No body part; possibly from ancient Greek voting with beans, to give away a secret.
Idioms that mention a body part.Under the weather: Nautical origin: sick sailors went below deck, away from the weather above.
Idioms that mention a body part.Once in a blue moon: A blue moon is a second full moon in one month, which happens about every two and a half years.
Idioms that mention a body part.Hit the sack: The sack is a bed, once a bag stuffed with straw, and no body part is involved.
Idioms that mention a body part.Bite the bullet: Often linked to soldiers biting on bullets during surgery without anesthesia, with no body part named.
Idioms that mention a body part.Cut corners: No body part, and it likely comes from tailors or craftsmen saving effort by skipping steps.
Idioms that mention a body part.Hit the hay: Hay was the old mattress stuffing, so hitting it meant going to bed.
Idioms that mention a body part.The last straw: It comes from 'the straw that broke the camel's back', and mentions no body part.
Idioms that mention a body part.Break the ice: Icebreaker ships cut literal ice, but the idiom means easing social tension, with no body part.
Idioms that mention a body part.Beat around the bush: Hunters beat bushes to flush out game, so beating around the bush means avoiding the point.
Idioms that mention a body part.Call it a day: It means to stop working for the day, and no body part is mentioned.

Things that would ruin a picnic.Ants: A picnic ant leaves a pheromone trail after finding crumbs so the colony follows in a line, so one scout soon becomes hundreds.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Rain: Even a light shower can soak the food and blanket in minutes, which is why picnics in rainy places are planned with backup dates.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Wasps: Wasps are drawn to sugary drinks and meat, and unlike honeybees they can sting multiple times.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Thunderstorm: Lightning kills around 20 people a year in the US, and the safest course is to go indoors right away.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Seagulls: Gulls near coasts have learned to snatch food from picnickers, and one study found they back off if you stare at them.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Bear: Bears can smell food from kilometers away, and a bear in a picnic area is a real worry in parts of North America.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Mud puddle: A puddle turns a blanket into a muddy mess and soaks shoes, and it is a classic picnic-ruiner after a rain.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Hailstorm: Hailstones form when updrafts carry raindrops high into the freezing air, and some grow as big as grapefruits.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Mosquitoes: Only female mosquitoes bite, because they need the protein in blood to produce their eggs; males feed on nectar.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Flies: A fly tastes with its feet and spits digestive fluid onto food, so a picnic with flies is no fun.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Strong wind: Strong wind blows away plates and napkins, and one reason picnickers weigh down blankets with food baskets.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Raccoon: Raccoons have sensitive front paws and clever hands and will open picnic baskets and coolers in the night.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Sandwiches: The sandwich is named after the Earl of Sandwich in the 1700s, and picnic lunches are the sandwich's natural home.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Lemonade: Lemonade has been sold in Paris since the 1600s, and it is a refreshing classic picnic drink.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Picnic blanket: A picnic blanket marks your spot, and the word picnic comes from French pique-nique in the 1600s.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Basket: A wicker basket is lightweight and sturdy, and it became the standard picnic carrier in the Victorian age.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Sunshine: Sunshine is the ideal picnic weather, though too much can melt the butter and wilt the salad.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Strawberries: A strawberry is not a true berry but an aggregate fruit, and it is the only fruit with its seeds on the outside.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Cheese: Cheese is a classic picnic staple, and it tastes best at room temperature, but it can sweat and spoil in strong sun.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Grapes: Grapes are a picnic favorite since they come in their own packaging, and a bunch needs no cutting or plates.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Watermelon: A watermelon is about 92 percent water, so a cold slice cools you down on a hot day at the picnic.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Cookies: Cookies are sturdy, so they survive the trip in a basket, and the word comes from the Dutch koekje, meaning little cake.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Shady tree: A shady tree keeps the sun off your food and head, and a big tree can cool the ground by several degrees.
Things that would ruin a picnic.Napkins: Napkins have been used since Roman times, and the Romans brought their own cloths to feasts.

Things at a circus.Clown: Clowns date back to ancient Egypt and Greece, but the red-nose white-face circus clown was created by Joseph Grimaldi in the early 1800s.
Things at a circus.Trapeze: A trapeze artist's catch often depends on timing within a fraction of a second; the first flying trapeze act was in 1859 by Jules Léotard.
Things at a circus.Ringmaster: The ringmaster traditionally led the circus ring, which is about 13 metres in diameter, a size set by horse riding needs.
Things at a circus.Tightrope: Tightrope walking has been around since ancient times, and in 1974 Philippe Petit walked between the Twin Towers.
Things at a circus.Juggler: Jugglers have performed since ancient Egypt, as seen on tomb paintings about 4,000 years old.
Things at a circus.Big top: The big top is a huge tent; Barnum's circus tents held thousands of spectators and took a crew to raise.
Things at a circus.Unicycle: A unicycle has one wheel and no brakes, and riders can even use them to play basketball or hockey.
Things at a circus.Human cannonball: A human cannonball was first shot in London in 1877; the act is powered by springs or compressed air, not gunpowder.
Things at a circus.Strongman: Strongmen drew crowds in the 1800s, and many lifted impressive weights by showmanship as well as brute strength.
Things at a circus.Popcorn: Popcorn is a circus staple, and it was a favourite at fairs even before movie theatres sold it.
Things at a circus.Stilts: Stilts date back to ancient times; stilt walkers hold weight on their feet strapped to long wooden poles.
Things at a circus.Acrobat: Acrobats train for years; the human pyramid is among the oldest circus acts and needs perfect balance.
Things at a circus.Judge's gavel: A judge's gavel is courtroom gear, not circus; there's no trick, just a wooden hammer for calling order.
Things at a circus.Snowplow: A snowplow clears roads in winter, and you won't find one in a circus tent.
Things at a circus.Lighthouse: A lighthouse guides ships along the coast, and the tallest ones are over 100 metres tall.
Things at a circus.Submarine: Submarines dive deep, and the first military one was used in the American Revolution.
Things at a circus.Tractor: Tractors power farms, and the first gas-powered ones appeared in the 1890s.
Things at a circus.Dentist's drill: A dentist's drill spins up to hundreds of thousands of revolutions per minute, nothing like a circus act.
Things at a circus.Fax machine: The fax machine was invented in the 1840s, over 30 years before the telephone.
Things at a circus.Hospital bed: A hospital bed adjusts with motors, and you'd find it in a hospital, not under a big top.
Things at a circus.Bank vault: A bank vault's door can weigh tonnes, and some are time-locked so they can't be opened out of hours.
Things at a circus.Voting booth: A voting booth offers privacy for the secret ballot, an idea that spread from Australia in the 1850s.
Things at a circus.Igloo: An igloo is built from snow blocks, and inside it can be 15 to 20 degrees warmer than outside.
Things at a circus.Oil rig: An oil rig drills far under the sea, and the biggest ones are as tall as skyscrapers.

Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Knight: A knight trained from boyhood as page and squire, and the full armour of the late Middle Ages could weigh around 20 to 25 kilograms.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Squire: A squire was a knight's apprentice who cared for his armour and horse, and fought beside him, until being knighted himself.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Jester: Jesters were paid to joke freely, and a few were the only people in court who could safely tell a king hard truths.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Steward: The steward ran the household and estate, managing food, servants and accounts, and was often the lord's most trusted officer.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Cook: Castle cooks fed hundreds in great halls, roasting meat on spits, and spices were costly status symbols at a lord's table.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Page: A page was a boy of about seven who served in a noble household, the first step on the road toward knighthood.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Falconer: Falconers trained hunting birds, and medieval law even linked which bird you could fly to your rank in society.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Chamberlain: The chamberlain looked after the lord's private rooms and finances, a title that survives today in royal households.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Archer: Castle archers defended walls through arrow slits, and the English longbow could pierce armour at close range.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Minstrel: Minstrels travelled between courts with songs and stories, spreading news and legends such as tales of King Arthur.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Blacksmith: The castle blacksmith made and mended weapons, tools and horseshoes, and was crucial to any lord's fighting force.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Stable boy: Stable boys looked after the horses, valuable war steeds that could cost more than a farm worker earned in years.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Astronaut: No castle sent anyone to space, and the first astronaut orbit only came in 1961, well after any castle's working life.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Barista: Coffee only reached Europe in the 1600s, so a barista is far too late; medieval castles drank ale, wine and mead.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Programmer: Programmers need computers, which arrived centuries later, though medieval clockmakers did build complex mechanisms.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Influencer: Influencers need social media, so this job is only a few years old and not in any castle.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Taxi driver: Taxis appeared in the 1600s and 1800s, so no castle had a taxi driver, only grooms and carters.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Electrician: Electricians had no work before electric power in the 1800s, so castles were lit by torches and candles.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Mechanic: The word mechanic did exist, but it usually meant a manual worker, and a modern car mechanic came with cars much later.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Photographer: Photography was invented in the 1800s, so any picture of a castle's life then was painted or drawn by hand.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.DJ: DJs need recorded music and sound systems, a 20th-century invention, so minstrels had to play live.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Pilot: Pilots need aircraft, which only flew from 1903, so no castle had one on staff.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Telephonist: Telephonists connected calls, and the telephone dates from the 1870s, centuries after most castles served their purpose.
Jobs that existed in a medieval castle.Radiographer: Radiographers use X-rays, discovered in 1895, so castle surgeons worked with no way to see inside the body.

Things in a hair salon.Salon chair: Salon chairs pump up and down with a hydraulic foot lever, so the stylist can set the height for every client.
Things in a hair salon.Wash basin: A salon basin has a cut-out for the neck, so clients can lean back for shampooing without a sore neck.
Things in a hair salon.Mirror: Salon mirrors let clients watch every cut, and stylists often show the back with a second hand mirror.
Things in a hair salon.Hood dryer: A hood dryer blows warm air over rollers or perms so hair sets while the client sits and reads.
Things in a hair salon.Rollers: Rollers hold hair in a curl while it cools or dries, because hydrogen bonds in the hair reset as it dries.
Things in a hair salon.Hair dye: Permanent dye opens the hair cuticle with ammonia and peroxide, forming color inside the strand that lasts until the hair is cut.
Things in a hair salon.Foils: Foils separate the strands being bleached or colored for highlights, so the product doesn't touch the rest of the hair.
Things in a hair salon.Clippers: The numbered guards on clippers show the length in eighths of an inch, so a number 4 leaves half an inch.
Things in a hair salon.Hair straightener: Flat irons heat hair to about 150 to 230 degrees Celsius to reshape it, which is why heat-protectant sprays exist.
Things in a hair salon.Styling gel: Gel dries into a stiff film around each strand, which is why gelled hair feels crunchy until you scrunch it.
Things in a hair salon.Salon cape: The cape keeps cut hair off your clothes, and a neck snap or clip holds it in place so strands don't fall down your collar.
Things in a hair salon.Dental chair: A dental chair reclines like a salon wash chair but holds a drill and a light. It belongs in a dentist's office.
Things in a hair salon.Car lift: A car lift is a mechanic's equipment. Salon chairs are raised by a lever, not a lift for vehicles.
Things in a hair salon.Anvil: An anvil is the iron block a blacksmith hammers metal on. A stylist's station is quite far from a forge.
Things in a hair salon.Kiln: A kiln fires pottery at over 1,000 degrees Celsius, far hotter than any salon tool, and belongs in a potter's studio.
Things in a hair salon.Jury box: A jury box is the railed seating for jurors in court. The only judging in a salon happens at the mirror.
Things in a hair salon.Pulpit: A pulpit is the raised stand a preacher speaks from. A stylist's podium is the salon chair, raised by a lever.
Things in a hair salon.Fire pole: A fire pole lets firefighters slide down from the upper floor of a station, and no salon is built for that.
Things in a hair salon.Hay bale: A hay bale is tightly bound dried grass, stacked on farms to feed livestock. Salons stock hair products instead.
Things in a hair salon.Operating table: Operating tables are for surgeons, not stylists, even if some haircuts feel like major surgery.
Things in a hair salon.Bunk bed: Bunk beds stack two sleepers in dorms and cabins. A salon has chairs and basins, and no beds at all.
Things in a hair salon.Slot machine: Slot machines are casino gambling devices that pay out coins. At a salon the only thing paid out is a new look.
Things in a hair salon.Pottery wheel: A pottery wheel spins clay for a potter. A salon wheel spins only the stylist's cart of tools.
Things in a hair salon.Pizza oven: A pizza oven can reach about 400 degrees Celsius, much hotter than any salon device. It belongs in a pizzeria.

Things that make their own light.Firefly: Fireflies make light through a chemical reaction in their abdomen that is nearly 100% efficient, producing almost no heat.
Things that make their own light.Glow stick: A glow stick works by chemiluminescence: snapping the inner vial mixes two chemicals that react and glow without heat.
Things that make their own light.The Sun: The Sun's light comes from nuclear fusion in its core, and takes tens of thousands of years to reach the surface but just over 8 minutes to reach Earth.
Things that make their own light.Lightning: A bolt heats the air to around 30,000 kelvin, hotter than the Sun's surface, and the flash makes the thunder.
Things that make their own light.Lava: Molten lava glows by incandescence, meaning the heat itself makes the light, at temperatures around 700 to 1,200 degrees Celsius.
Things that make their own light.Anglerfish: Deep-sea anglerfish dangle a lure with glowing bacteria, which they use to attract prey in the dark.
Things that make their own light.Glow worm: Glow worms are beetle larvae or fungus gnat larvae that make their own light; in New Zealand caves, they hang by the thousands.
Things that make their own light.Campfire: Flames glow because hot soot particles emit light, which is why yellow flames contain carbon.
Things that make their own light.Candle flame: A candle flame is hottest in its pale blue base, while the yellow glow comes from glowing soot particles.
Things that make their own light.Sirius: Sirius is the brightest star in the night sky, about 8.6 light-years away and twice as massive as the Sun.
Things that make their own light.Neon sign: The glow comes from gas excited by electricity, and neon itself gives red-orange; other colors use argon and phosphors.
Things that make their own light.Fireworks: Their colors come from metal salts: strontium gives red, barium green, and copper blue.
Things that make their own light.The Moon: The Moon makes no light of its own and only reflects sunlight, reflecting roughly 12 percent.
Things that make their own light.Mirror: A mirror reflects light but does not produce any, so in a dark room it shows nothing.
Things that make their own light.Diamond: Diamonds sparkle by bending and reflecting light, so they stay dark without a light source.
Things that make their own light.Venus: Venus is the brightest planet, but its brilliance is reflected sunlight from its thick clouds.
Things that make their own light.Disco ball: A disco ball reflects the lights that hit it, so it shines only when a spotlight does.
Things that make their own light.Bike reflector: Reflectors bounce a car's headlights straight back using tiny prisms, but have no light source.
Things that make their own light.Cat's eyes: A cat's eyes shine at night due to the tapetum lucidum, a layer that reflects light back, but it makes none.
Things that make their own light.Glitter: Glitter sparkles by reflecting light, and in the dark it goes dim.
Things that make their own light.Snow: Snow is bright because its crystals scatter light, but it is not a source.
Things that make their own light.Tinfoil: Foil reflects light like a mirror and can't glow on its own.
Things that make their own light.Sequins: Sequins catch the light and bounce it around, but only if there's light to catch.
Things that make their own light.Gold: Gold shines through reflection, and it does not emit light unless it is heated until it glows.

Things that generate electricity.Electric eel: An electric eel can produce up to about 600 volts, and it's not a true eel but a knifefish.
Things that generate electricity.Battery: The first battery, built by Alessandro Volta in 1800, was a stack of metal disks and brine-soaked cloth called the voltaic pile.
Things that generate electricity.Lightning: A lightning bolt carries hundreds of millions of volts but lasts only a fraction of a second, and it's hotter than the Sun's surface.
Things that generate electricity.Solar panel: Solar panels turn light directly into electricity through the photovoltaic effect, first noted in 1839.
Things that generate electricity.Wind turbine: A modern turbine blade can be longer than a football field, and one spin of a big rotor can power a home for a day.
Things that generate electricity.Power plant: Most power plants, from coal to nuclear, just boil water to spin a turbine.
Things that generate electricity.Generator: A generator turns motion into electricity using Faraday's discovery that moving a magnet near a coil creates current.
Things that generate electricity.Hydroelectric dam: Hydroelectric dams supply about 15 percent of world electricity, and the Three Gorges Dam is the largest.
Things that generate electricity.Electric ray: Electric rays stun prey with shocks, and ancient Greeks used them to numb pain.
Things that generate electricity.Fuel cell: A fuel cell makes electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen, and its only emission is water.
Things that generate electricity.Bike dynamo: A bike dynamo is a small generator, driven by the wheel, that powers the lights while you pedal.
Things that generate electricity.Light bulb: A light bulb uses electricity, and old incandescent ones turn most of it into heat.
Things that generate electricity.Toaster: Toasters use electricity to heat nichrome wire, and they were invented in 1893.
Things that generate electricity.Television: A television consumes electricity, and early sets used a cathode ray tube.
Things that generate electricity.Electric fence: An electric fence is powered, and it delivers a short harmless shock to teach animals to stay away.
Things that generate electricity.Refrigerator: A refrigerator uses electricity to move heat out of the box, and it runs all day.
Things that generate electricity.Hair dryer: A hair dryer uses a heating coil and a fan, and uses a lot of power for a small device.
Things that generate electricity.Extension cord: An extension cord only carries electricity and doesn't create any.
Things that generate electricity.Power outlet: A power outlet delivers electricity but doesn't make it, and the plug designs differ across over a dozen types worldwide.
Things that generate electricity.Fuse: A fuse protects a circuit, and it melts if the current gets too high.
Things that generate electricity.Electric guitar: An electric guitar converts string vibration into a tiny electrical signal through magnetic pickups.
Things that generate electricity.Ceiling fan: A ceiling fan uses a motor and electricity, and it cools people by moving air, not the room.
Things that generate electricity.Microwave: A microwave oven was invented after a radar engineer noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket.
Things that generate electricity.Doorbell: A doorbell uses electricity, usually at a low voltage from a small transformer.

Things at the beach.Sandcastle: A good sandcastle needs damp sand, about one part water to eight parts sand, and big competitions award prizes for sculptures several metres tall.
Things at the beach.Lifeguard: Lifeguards watch for rip currents, which cause the majority of beach rescues and are best escaped by swimming parallel to shore.
Things at the beach.Seashell: A shell is the home of a mollusc, and holding one up to your ear doesn't capture the sea, just ambient noise resonating.
Things at the beach.Sunscreen: SPF 30 blocks about 97% of UVB rays, not twice as much as SPF 15, and it needs reapplying every two hours.
Things at the beach.Beach towel: Cotton towels trace back to Turkey's loops, and the sand sticking to your wet skin gets a lot worse than on dry skin.
Things at the beach.Bucket and spade: A classic seaside pair, and British seaside tradition tied buckets and spades to Victorian holidays when rail trips reached coasts.
Things at the beach.Parasol: The word comes from Italian for 'against the sun', and parasols were a status symbol in ancient China, Egypt, and Rome.
Things at the beach.Surfboard: Surfing began in Polynesia, and ancient Hawaiian boards could be 5 metres long and made of wood from koa trees.
Things at the beach.Seaweed: Seaweed is algae, not a plant, and it supplies much of the oxygen we breathe along with the rest of the ocean's algae.
Things at the beach.Sand dune: Dunes move with the wind, and some, called singing dunes, hum or boom when sand grains slide down.
Things at the beach.Tide pool: Creatures in rock pools survive huge swings in temperature and salinity twice a day as the tide moves in and out.
Things at the beach.Flip-flops: They echo ancient Egyptian sandals from around 4,000 years ago, and the name imitates the sound they make.
Things at the beach.Deck chair: The folding chair got its name from ocean liners, where passengers lounged on the deck, and the British seaside adopted it.
Things at the beach.Ski lift: Hauls skiers up snow slopes, so nothing to do with a beach, unless you count a few indoor and desert resorts.
Things at the beach.Igloo: The Inuit snow house is built of blocks cut from compacted snow, and body heat alone can warm the inside to above freezing.
Things at the beach.Sled: Used on snow and ice, and sleds have been around for thousands of years, with some ancient ones found in Scandinavia.
Things at the beach.Icicle: Forms when meltwater drips and refreezes, and the longest icicles can grow several metres in cold spots.
Things at the beach.Fireplace: A hearth for cold living rooms, not hot sand, though beach bonfires use the same flames.
Things at the beach.Snow globe: Invented in France in the 1800s, and the first one at the 1878 Paris Exposition included a tiny model of the Eiffel Tower.
Things at the beach.Ice skates: Archaeologists found bone skates in Finland about 3,000 years ago, but they won't glide on warm sand.
Things at the beach.Earmuffs: A teenager, Chester Greenwood, patented earmuffs in 1877, and in Maine they're celebrated on a local holiday.
Things at the beach.Snowplow: It clears roads in winter, and a skier can also make a snowplow turn, but you won't see one on a beach.
Things at the beach.Snowman: The first known picture of a snowman dates to 1380 in a prayer book, and snowmen have melted ever since.
Things at the beach.Ski poles: Used for balance and rhythm, and poles don't help you on sand, though a few Nordic walkers use them anywhere.

Sportswear brands.Nike: Nike takes its name from the Greek goddess of victory, and the Swoosh logo was bought from a design student for only 35 dollars.
Sportswear brands.Adidas: Adi Dassler's company in Herzogenaurach gave Jesse Owens shoes at the 1936 Olympics, and the three stripes were bought from a Finnish brand.
Sportswear brands.Puma: Puma split from Adidas after a feud between brothers Adi and Rudolf Dassler, and the two firms still sit across a river from each other.
Sportswear brands.Reebok: The name comes from the Afrikaans word for a small African antelope, rhebok, and the brand began in Bolton, England.
Sportswear brands.Under Armour: Kevin Plank started it in 1996 as a football player looking for T-shirts that would stay dry, and began by selling out of his car.
Sportswear brands.New Balance: Founded in Boston in 1906 making arch supports, New Balance is one of the few big names still making some shoes in the US.
Sportswear brands.Asics: The name is an acronym of a Latin phrase meaning a sound mind in a sound body, and the brand is Japanese.
Sportswear brands.Fila: Fila began in Biella, Italy, making underwear and knitwear, and its sporty look later became a tennis and hip-hop staple.
Sportswear brands.Umbro: Founded in Cheshire, England, in 1924 as Humphreys Brothers, it shortened its name and became synonymous with football kits.
Sportswear brands.Lululemon: This Canadian label began in 1998 in Vancouver, helping make yoga pants everyday wear.
Sportswear brands.Speedo: The Australian brand's name came from an 1928 slogan, and its swimwear raced in several Olympics.
Sportswear brands.Gucci: Gucci is a luxury fashion brand from Florence, and not known for sports gear.
Sportswear brands.Prada: Prada is Milan luxury fashion, although its Linea Rossa line does sports.
Sportswear brands.Zara: Zara is a fast-fashion chain, rather than a sports brand.
Sportswear brands.Chanel: Chanel is Parisian haute couture, and no sports label.
Sportswear brands.Rolex: Rolex makes luxury watches, and was the first to produce a waterproof wristwatch in 1926, but is not sportswear.
Tiffany & Co. is best known for jewellery in its trademark robin's-egg blue box.
Sportswear brands.Levi's: Levi's is a jeans maker, not sportswear.
Sportswear brands.Ray-Ban: Ray-Ban is an eyewear brand whose Aviators were designed for American pilots in the 1930s.
Sportswear brands.Swatch: Swatch is a Swiss watch brand and not apparel.
Sportswear brands.Dior: Dior is Parisian couture, and its fame comes from the 1947 New Look.
Sportswear brands.Hermès: Hermès is a luxury house famed for its Birkin and Kelly bags.
Sportswear brands.Burberry: Burberry is a British trench-coat house, not a sports brand.
Sportswear brands.Cartier: Cartier is a French jeweller that made one of the first men's wristwatches, for an aviator friend in 1904.

Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Pooh: Named after Winnipeg, a Canadian black bear at London Zoo, and Christopher Robin's toy. A. A. Milne's real son owned the toys.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Piglet: A Very Small Animal, as Milne calls him. He's nervous, but proves a brave friend.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Eeyore: The gloomy donkey who loses his tail, which Pooh finds being used as a bell-pull at Owl's house.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Tigger: Tiggers bounce, and he doesn't appear until the second book, The House at Pooh Corner, in 1928.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Kanga: Roo's mother, who carries him in her pouch. Pooh's friends first fear she's a dangerous new arrival.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Roo: Kanga's baby kangaroo, who rides in her pouch. He's the smallest of the group, with a squeaky voice.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Owl: Milne spells his name "Wol." Everyone thinks he's wise, though he can barely spell.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Rabbit: The practical one, with lots of friends-and-relations. He often organizes everyone, and he's good at planning.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Christopher Robin: Based on Milne's real son, Christopher Robin Milne. The original toys now live in the New York Public Library.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Heffalumps: Pooh's imagined elephants, whom he tries to trap with a pot of honey. They're so frightening, he never actually meets one.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Gopher: A Disney addition from 1966 who whistles when he talks. He's not in Milne's original books.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Paddington: Michael Bond's bear from Darkest Peru who loves marmalade, a different beloved British bear.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Rupert: Rupert Bear is a British comic-strip bear from 1920 in the Daily Express, a different series.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Baloo: Baloo is the sleepy bear of Kipling's The Jungle Book, a different story from Winnie the Pooh.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Ratty: Ratty is a water vole in The Wind in the Willows, and not a character in Winnie the Pooh.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Peter Rabbit: Beatrix Potter's 1902 rabbit in a blue jacket, from a different series than Winnie the Pooh.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Mole: Mole is a shy, home-loving character in The Wind in the Willows, not in Winnie the Pooh.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Mr. Toad: Mr. Toad is the reckless, car-obsessed toad of The Wind in the Willows, not of Winnie the Pooh.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Babar: Babar the elephant was created by Jean de Brunhoff in 1931, in a different story series.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Corduroy: A toy bear in a department store, from Don Freeman's 1968 book, not from Winnie the Pooh.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Pingu: Pingu is a Swiss clay-animation penguin who speaks only gibberish, not from Winnie the Pooh.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Bagheera: The black panther of The Jungle Book who raises Mowgli, from a different series than Winnie the Pooh.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Stuart Little: E. B. White's 1945 story about a mouse born into a human family, not from Winnie the Pooh.
Characters in Winnie the Pooh.Fozzie: The Muppets' comic bear with a "wocka wocka" catchphrase, not a member of the Hundred Acre Wood.

Cat breeds (not dogs).Siamese: From Thailand, once Siam; their pigment is temperature-sensitive, so cooler extremities are darker.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Persian: A long-haired, flat-faced breed prized since the 1600s that needs daily grooming.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Maine Coon: One of the largest domestic cats, the state cat of Maine, with males sometimes over 8 kg.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Bengal: Bred from domestic cats and the Asian leopard cat for a wild look, and many enjoy water.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Ragdoll: Named for going limp when picked up; developed in California in the 1960s by Ann Baker.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Sphynx: Hairless through a natural mutation; it needs baths because skin oils build up.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Burmese: All modern Burmese descend from one cat, Wong Mau, brought to the US in 1930.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Abyssinian: With its ticked coat, legend ties it to Ethiopia, once Abyssinia, though genetics point to Southeast Asian coasts.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Russian Blue: A plush double-coated cat with green eyes, said to hail from Arkhangelsk in Russia.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Scottish Fold: Folded ears from a cartilage mutation, all traced to a barn cat named Susie found in Scotland in 1961.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Birman: The 'sacred cat of Burma' has white gloves on its paws; the temple legend is a folk tale.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Manx: Tailless thanks to a natural mutation on the Isle of Man.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Beagle: A scent hound with around 220 million scent receptors; Snoopy is one.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Poodle: Originally German water retrievers; the fancy clip had a purpose in cold water.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Boxer: A German breed; the name comes from how it uses its front paws.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Collie: Lassie was a rough collie, though played by male dogs.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Dachshund: The name means 'badger dog' in German, because it was bred to dig out badgers.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Whippet: Can sprint about 56 km/h, earning the nickname poor man's racehorse.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Pug: Bred as companions for Chinese emperors; a group of pugs is called a grumble.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Corgi: Queen Elizabeth II owned more than 30 corgis, mostly Pembroke Welsh Corgis.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Husky: Sled dogs of the Chukchi people; huskies ran the 1925 serum relay to Nome.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Chihuahua: The smallest dog breed, named for the Mexican state of Chihuahua.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Akita: A Japanese breed; Hachiko waited at Shibuya Station for nearly ten years for his owner.
Cat breeds (not dogs).Labrador: It came from Newfoundland, not Labrador, and was the top AKC breed for over 30 years.
